book.title: Playing to Win
book.author: A.G. Lafley and Roger L. Martin

chapters.title: Strategy Is Choice
chapters.hook: Six growth priorities, each one plausible. None of them knows what the others are doing.
chapters.counterintuition: The more goals you add to a strategic plan, the weaker the plan becomes. Not because focus is virtuous in itself, but because each goal that requires different customers, a different field, or different capabilities breaks the internal logic that makes strategy work. A list of intentions is not a cascade.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pull out any active plan you have. Pick the second-biggest priority and ask whether it requires different customers or capabilities than the first. A conflict there is where the cascade breaks.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A strategy only exists when five choices cohere: aspiration, field, advantage, capabilities, and systems all pointing in the same direction. A thorough list of priorities is not yet a strategy.

breakdown.fastRead:
Kate put three growth goals on the bakery whiteboard Thursday morning: wholesale accounts, a subscription box, and a second location by spring. Each one made sense. None of them pointed at the same wall.

She was not planning badly. She was planning well while skipping strategy.

Strategy is not a list of good ideas. It is a cascade of five choices that must cohere: what winning looks like, where you compete, how you beat alternatives there, what capabilities that requires, and what systems keep all of it reinforced. When the choices do not fit, the list is a wish.

Kate needed a choice, not a longer whiteboard.
breakdown.deepRead:
The cascade starts with what you are actually trying to win. Not a growth target. Not a vision statement. A specific choice about which customers you want to delight and which alternatives you intend to beat them on.

That first choice immediately shapes the second: where you will and will not compete, across geography, customer segment, channel, and category. The second shapes the third: what kind of advantage or value equation will beat the alternatives in that specific field. Capabilities come next, but not as a talent inventory. They are the specific things your organization must be able to do to deliver the how-to-win choice. The fifth choice is management systems: the reviews, measures, and accountability routines that reinforce all four prior choices. A strategy is not complete until all five are made and all five fit.

Olay did not recover because P&G invested harder in what the brand already was. It recovered because the choices fit: a clearer target customer, a sharper price position, a more attractive market segment, and capabilities that could deliver the new offer all pointed in the same direction at once. Changing any one of those choices would have pulled the others out of alignment.

That is the coherence test. Pick any choice in your current strategy document and ask: if I changed this, would it require me to change the others? If the answer is no, the choices are not connected. They are parallel aspirations sharing a page.

Now try it on your own priorities. Pick the second one. Ask whether it requires different customers than the first, a different field, or a different set of capabilities. A conflict there is where the cascade breaks.

A list of priorities, however ambitious, is not a strategy until the choices reinforce each other.
breakdown.fullRead:
A consulting partner opens the week with six new proposals in six different sectors: healthcare technology, environmental compliance, supply-chain logistics, public-sector procurement, commercial real estate advisory, and one more. Every proposal looks winnable. Every one requires a different set of client credentials, a different delivery model, and subject matter expertise the practice does not currently have.

He calls this a strong pipeline. There is no strategy here.

The difference becomes visible in what accumulates. A practice that wins in six sectors earns six one-time engagements. It does not earn the deep pattern-recognition in any single field that makes the next engagement there faster to win, cheaper to deliver, and more credible in the client's eyes. Each new sector is a restart from zero. The pipeline grows. The capability stands still.

A coherent where-to-play choice creates the opposite dynamic. Each engagement in the chosen field builds on the last. The referral network tightens. The practice develops the case examples, the regulatory familiarity, and the judgment that a generalist cannot replicate. That advantage compresses over time. It is only available to organizations that made a choice about where to compete.

Take a nonprofit that started with a clear workforce development mission and grew to nine programs in four years, each one added because a grant came through. Early childhood literacy. Emergency food assistance. Digital skills for adults. Housing navigation. Each one good at something. Together, they became a grant management company operating under a workforce banner. When the largest funder asked what the organization was best at, the honest answer was: whichever program the last check was written for.

A strategy is not what you say you are doing. A strategy is what the coherence of your choices reveals you are actually committed to.

The coherence test asks one question for every choice in the cascade: if I changed this, would it require me to change the others? If yes, the choices are connected. If no, they are a list.

Run the test on a typical planning document and most priorities survive the swap. The digital transformation initiative can be removed without changing the customer experience initiative. The talent program can be modified without touching the revenue target. Each one is a parallel track on its own trajectory. They share a page. They do not share a logic.

Now try it on your own work. Take the third priority you are currently running and ask: if I stopped it tomorrow, would anything else I am doing change? If the answer is no, that priority is not part of your strategy. It is a separate project running alongside it.

A software team once built infrastructure for three customer segments simultaneously. Every architecture decision optimized for one segment was challenged by advocates for the other two and resolved with a compromise that slightly served each while fully serving none. The product shipped. Users in all three segments were moderately satisfied. The team was exhausted by negotiations that had no resolution principle because the strategic choice at the top of the cascade was never made.

The cascade does not care how hard the team works. It cares whether the choices cohere.

Olay's recovery is the clean version. The choices pointed in the same direction: one customer type, one market position, one advantage logic, one capability system built to deliver it. Once those choices fit, every subsequent decision had a resolution principle. The product team knew who they were building for. The pricing team knew what position to hold. Execution became faster and less contentious because the cascade had already resolved most of the arguments.

That is what a coherent strategy gives you. Not a guarantee of winning. A resolution principle for trade-offs. And trade-offs arrive every day, at every level, whether or not you have named your cascade.

Name the cascade. Then check whether it coheres. That is where strategy begins.

examples.title: Claire Counts What Three Goals Actually Require
examples.scenario: 'Can we add a fourth tier?' the line cook calls at 7:50 a.m. Claire is at the bakery counter with a wholesale proposal, flour still on her apron. Three goals are on the whiteboard: more wholesale accounts, a subscription box, a second location by spring. Wholesale needs a delivery van and a sales rep. The box needs a packing station. The location needs a manager and six months of cash. None of the three overlap. She must decide before the flour delivery at nine which goal gets this month's reinvestment.
examples.whatToDo: Name which of the three goals fits the bakery's current capability (delivery, packaging, or a second kitchen) and fund only that one. The other two go on hold until the cascade from the first choice is stable.
examples.whyItMatters: Three growth goals each requiring different customers, capabilities, and capital are three separate strategies. Pursuing all three simultaneously means none of them gets enough resources to cohere.

examples.title: Thomas Sees What the Program List Became
examples.scenario: It took Thomas three budget cycles to notice the pattern. The nonprofit had added six programs in four years, each one triggered by a grant opportunity, not a strategic choice. The list had grown from three programs to nine, each serving a different population under a different theory of change. He has an annual impact report due in a week and must decide whether to present all nine programs as a coherent portfolio or acknowledge, for the first time, that the cascade has dissolved into funder management.
examples.whatToDo: Before writing the impact report, trace each program back to the original aspiration. Any program whose origin was a grant opportunity rather than the stated mission signals that the cascade needs to be rebuilt.
examples.whyItMatters: A portfolio shaped by incoming grants has replaced the strategic cascade with a set of funder priorities. The impact report cannot fix that, but naming it honestly is the first step toward building a coherent field choice.

examples.title: Etienne's Pipeline Has Six Proposals and No Strategy
examples.scenario: At 9:14 a.m. Monday, Etienne opens a shared drive with six new proposals in six different sectors. Each one was won on a different partner's personal relationship with a new industry client. He must decide before the two o'clock pipeline review which sectors to pursue and which to cut. The practice has never lost a proposal. It has also never built repeatable capability in any single sector. Every engagement is a restart from scratch.
examples.whatToDo: Pick the one or two sectors where the practice's existing delivery record creates a real edge over generalists. Decline proposals that require building credentials from zero until the first sector choice is stable.
examples.whyItMatters: Six sectors means six fresh starts. Revenue grows but capability stays flat. Without a coherent field choice, the practice cannot build the pattern-recognition that makes each next engagement faster to win and stronger to deliver.

examples.title: Luca Asks Which Listener the Station Is Winning
examples.scenario: Which listener is the station trying to win: the one who left for a podcast three years ago or the one who never found the station? Luca brings the question to the programming committee predicting quick consensus. After sixty minutes of debate, no one agrees. He realizes the current split format is not a programming choice. It is the documented result of a strategic decision that was never made.
examples.whatToDo: Name which listener type the station is competing for in the next eighteen months. Every scheduling, staffing, and production decision should follow from that one choice, not be made independently of it.
examples.whyItMatters: A format serving two incompatible audiences with one production budget serves neither well. Without naming which listener the station is competing to win, every quarterly format review restarts the same argument from zero.

examples.title: Hadiya Sees What the Job Description Actually Says
examples.scenario: The department conference room at 4:15 p.m. on a Tuesday in March: one hire budget, two printed job descriptions, twelve criteria total. Before: Hadiya submits the description with six research-aligned criteria and six teaching-aligned criteria, hoping to attract a candidate who can do both. After: the shortlist produces candidates mediocre in both directions, and she sees that the description was a symptom of a strategic choice the department had never made.
examples.whatToDo: Choose which aspiration drives the hire: graduate ranking or undergraduate quality: rewrite the description from that choice alone. Criteria pointing two directions attract candidates who fit neither.
examples.whyItMatters: A job description split between two aspirations signals the underlying strategic choice was never made. The resulting hire partially serves both directions and fully serves neither.

examples.title: James Traces Three Years of Reactive Inventory
examples.scenario: Twelve pallets of slow-moving inventory fill the storeroom, each bought in the last three years to match a competitor's promotion. James has run the hardware store for eleven years. He traces the inventory purchase by purchase and finds that every decision was reactive: matching a competitor's move and not advancing a coherent position for any customer type. The store stocked for everyone and has loyalty from no one.
examples.whatToDo: Name the one customer type the store's location, staff knowledge, and relationship capacity could serve better than any competitor in the area. Stop carrying inventory optimized for the other types.
examples.whyItMatters: Stocking for every customer means competing against the chain's selection and the specialist's depth simultaneously. That position wins nothing. Coherent field choice means the inventory, staff, and service all point at the same customer.

questions.prompt: When a company has a vision statement, a growth target, a prioritized list of twelve initiatives, and a detailed annual budget, which of these is most likely to be confused with strategy itself?
choices: None of them; a strategy requires five mutually reinforcing choices, not any single element.
The growth target, because it names what the company is trying to achieve.
The 90-day plan, because it shows what the company will actually do.
questions.explanation: A strategy requires five reinforcing choices. A growth target is an aspiration, a plan is an execution schedule, and an initiatives list is a set of priorities. None becomes strategy until all five choices cohere around a specific field, advantage, capability system, and management logic.

questions.prompt: The boutique hotel had been known as a quiet weekend retreat for couples. This year, it added a kids' menu, a small conference room, and a happy-hour bar. Each addition came with reasonable demand evidence. What is the strategic risk of this pattern?
choices: Accept all three additions because each individually improves revenue.
Identify which addition best fits the original positioning and invest only in that one.
Hire a larger marketing team to promote all three new offerings simultaneously.
questions.explanation: The hotel's original positioning as a couples retreat defines one customer. Each addition targeting a different customer type breaks the cascade. Testing each addition against the original aspiration before committing keeps the five choices coherent and prevents the offer from drifting toward everyone.

questions.prompt: If a law firm's new strategic plan lists twelve priorities (digital modernization, lateral partner recruiting, sector expansion, AI tooling, junior training, branding refresh, alumni network, regional offices, alternative fee structures, knowledge management, DEI, partner compensation reform), what coherence test would distinguish strategy from a wish list?
choices: Approve it; twelve priorities show breadth and strategic ambition.
Rank the priorities by projected revenue and cut to the top five.
Test whether the twelve choices cohere: whether each choice enables and constrains the others.
questions.explanation: Cutting by revenue is execution triage, not strategy. The coherence test asks whether removing any choice would weaken the others. A list where each priority can be swapped without affecting the rest has no shared logic and is not yet a strategy, just a collection of partners' preferences.

questions.prompt: A software product serves enterprise clients who need security and dedicated support, and consumer users who need simplicity and low price. The team is scoping a new authentication feature. What strategic question should they ask first?
choices: Which customer type does this feature most reinforce, and is that the customer the strategy is built around?
Which customer type represents the larger addressable market, and would prioritizing that segment generate enough volume to absorb the per-account support costs the smaller segment requires?
Which customer type pays a higher price per seat, and would concentrating on that segment generate the margin the product needs to fund the capability investments the strategy requires?
questions.explanation: Market size and seat revenue are financial metrics, not strategic ones. The strategic question is whether the feature reinforces the chosen customer and advantage. Building for two incompatible customer types prevents the capability system from pointing in one direction and weakens both simultaneously.

questions.prompt: When a nonprofit's program list grew from three to nine in four years, with each new program triggered by a different funder's grant, what diagnosis best fits the underlying pattern?
choices: The nonprofit has a strong opportunistic culture and is funding its growth effectively, since each new program is paired with the grant that pays for it and so does not strain the organization's existing budget.
The five-choice cascade has collapsed: the portfolio is shaped by funder priorities, not by a coherent aspiration and field choice.

The nonprofit needs a better fundraising strategy to reduce its dependence on grants, because a diversified donor base would let the leadership pick programs on mission grounds instead of following funder priorities.
questions.explanation: Grant-driven program addition substitutes funder agendas for the organization's own cascade. Growth without a coherent aspiration and field choice produces a portfolio where programs compete for staff and resources instead of building on each other toward a single winning position.

questions.prompt: The consulting practice wins engagements in six different sectors each year, with no sector representing more than twenty percent of revenue. Senior partners argue that the diversification is a strength. What is the strategic objection to this view?
choices: The practice is dangerously dependent on individual partners for all its revenue.
The practice needs a stronger marketing function to attract clients without personal relationships.
There is no coherent where-to-play choice, so no capability or credential can accumulate in any sector.
questions.explanation: Partner dependency is a talent risk, not the strategic failure here. Without a chosen field, every engagement is a restart in unfamiliar territory. A practice that builds no sector depth cannot develop the pattern-recognition, case examples, or referral network that would make the next engagement there faster, stronger, or cheaper.

questions.prompt: A manager tests her company's five strategic priorities with the coherence question and finds that each priority could be changed or removed without requiring any changes to the others. What does this test reveal?
choices: The five priorities lack internal logic; they are parallel tracks sharing a document, not a strategy cascade.
The strategy is well-designed; independent priorities allow the company to adapt faster to changing conditions.
The manager should add more priorities to create stronger connections between the existing ones.
questions.explanation: Independent priorities with no mutual dependence form a list. A real cascade means each choice constrains and enables the others. Five priorities that can each be swapped without disturbing the rest give the organization no resolution principle when trade-offs appear; every conflict is litigated from scratch.

questions.prompt: When a department must choose between growing graduate rankings through research hires or deepening undergraduate engagement through teaching-focused hires, why is hiring a candidate who claims to do both moderately well the most expensive option?
choices: A candidate with both strengths will cost too much for the department's budget, since dual-skilled professors command salaries higher than the department's current hiring band allows for a tenure-track appointment.

Such a dual-strength candidate is unlikely to be found in the current market, because the academic pipeline rewards specialization and produces few faculty who can credibly contribute to both research output and undergraduate engagement at a high level.
The hybrid hire defers the strategic choice and produces a result that partially serves two directions rather than fully advancing either.
questions.explanation: The hybrid hire feels like a creative solution but avoids the cascade decision. Choosing between graduate ranking and undergraduate quality requires commitment because the capabilities, measures, and downstream resource allocations for each direction differ. A hire serving both ends reinforces neither, and the cascade remains unresolved after the hire.

questions.prompt: The regional bakery owner has three growth goals: more wholesale accounts, a monthly subscription box, and a second retail location. Each is defensible in isolation. What is the right way to choose among them?
choices: Pursue all three at reduced investment to test which one gains traction first, since a portfolio approach reduces the risk of committing capacity to a single direction that may not work in the bakery's local market.
Pick the goal whose capability requirements best fit the bakery's current activity system and the field it wants to own.

Choose the goal with the highest projected revenue for the next twelve months, because cash flow improvement gives the bakery owner the financial cushion needed to fund the longer-horizon capability investments later.
questions.explanation: Revenue projection tests financial attractiveness, not strategic fit. The three goals are structurally different businesses in terms of customer, capability, and channel. Funding the one that fits the current activity system creates a coherent foundation. Spreading across all three produces partial infrastructure for each and strategic advantage in none.

reviewCards.front: Your plan has five bold priorities and none of them require the team to stop doing anything. What does that tell you?
reviewCards.back: It signals the priorities are not yet a strategy. A real cascade requires choices that constrain each other: when you add one, the others limit it. A list where everything can coexist without conflict has no internal logic.

reviewCards.front: What are the five choices in a strategy cascade?
reviewCards.back: Winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, the required capabilities, and management systems; each one enabling and constraining the others. A strategy is only complete when all five cohere.

reviewCards.front: A consulting practice wins in a new sector every quarter but builds no reputation in any of them. What strategic choice is missing?
reviewCards.back: A where-to-play choice. Without naming which field to compete in, each engagement is a restart from zero. No capability, credential, or referral network accumulates to create an advantage that compounds over time.

reviewCards.front: What is the coherence test for a strategy?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether changing any one choice would require you to change the others. If the choices can each be swapped independently without disturbing the rest, they are not connected; you have a list, not a cascade.

reviewCards.front: What made the Olay turnaround work strategically?
reviewCards.back: The choices fit each other: a clearer target customer, a sharper price position, a more attractive market segment, and capabilities that could deliver the new offer all pointed in the same direction. Coherence, not increased investment in the existing approach.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish a strategy cascade from a list of priorities by testing whether the choices reinforce each other. You practice the coherence test: asking whether each choice in a plan would require changing the others if it were modified. A plan passes when the choices constrain each other. A list fails when each priority can be swapped without disturbing the rest.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a business or team plan
ifThenPlans.plan: If any priority in the plan could be removed or swapped without requiring changes to the others, name the coherence gap before approving the document.

ifThenPlans.context: considering a new opportunity
ifThenPlans.plan: If the new opportunity requires a different customer, field, or capability than the current strategy, treat it as a second strategy and evaluate it on its own terms, not added to the existing cascade.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a growth proposal with multiple goals
ifThenPlans.plan: If the proposal lists goals that each require different customers and capabilities, decide which one fits the current cascade before committing resources to any of them.

ifThenPlans.context: hiring or allocating budget
ifThenPlans.plan: If a hire or budget allocation is being justified by two incompatible strategic aspirations simultaneously, the underlying cascade choice has not been made; resolve the cascade first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one project or initiative you are currently running. Trace it backward through the cascade: does it require a specific field choice, a specific advantage logic, specific capabilities, and specific reinforcing systems? Name any link in the chain that is missing or vague. That gap is where your strategy currently stops.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, take one team decision you made and ask whether it reinforced a coherent cascade or implicitly started a parallel one. If it started a parallel one, name that explicitly and decide whether the strategy should shift toward it or the decision should be reversed.

chapters.title: What Is Winning
chapters.hook: An aspiration statement sat at the top of the planning document, unchanged for four years. Every new initiative fit it. None of them had to. That is the problem with playing to play.
chapters.counterintuition: The aspiration most people write sounds strong because it accepts everything. That acceptance is the sign it is not doing strategic work. An aspiration that fits every option equally has no edge to cut with.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write the aspiration your current project or role is working toward. Then ask it two questions: which specific customer would choose you over the alternative, and what specific alternative are you trying to beat? If neither question has a concrete answer, the aspiration is still playing to play.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A winning aspiration names which customers to delight and which alternatives to beat them on specifically enough that it can say no to a plausible-looking option. An aspiration that cannot say no is still playing to play.

breakdown.fastRead:
Stefan ran a food truck serving delicious, fresh food for everyone in the lunch crowd. In one week he received three growth opportunities: a catering contract for evening corporate events, a weekend slot at the farmers market, and a recurring lunchtime spot at a construction site two miles away.

Each opportunity looked promising. His aspiration said yes to all three.

Stefan was not choosing between good options. He was choosing between three options his aspiration had no basis for evaluating.

When he rewrote the aspiration as the best affordable hot lunch for workers who cannot leave the job site, the farmers market slot fell away immediately: wrong customer, wrong schedule. The catering contract did the same: wrong hour, wrong crowd. The construction site slot was not just acceptable. It was the only option his strategy required him to pursue.

An aspiration specific enough to say no is a strategy. Everything else is a list of things you would be willing to do.
breakdown.deepRead:
The distinction between a winning aspiration and a participation aspiration is not ambition. It is specificity.

A participation aspiration sounds like this: be a good alternative for customers who want a different option. It names what the organization wants to avoid (losing customers to alternatives) without naming which customers, which alternatives, or what specific advantage would make this organization the better choice for that customer in that field.

Saturn was built on that kind of aspiration. GM's goal for the brand was to give American buyers a domestic alternative to the imports they were choosing. The aspiration named the problem (import competition) and the solution category (a domestic car) but left open which buyers, which price point, and what specific advantage would make a Saturn buyer choose Saturn again. Saturn's aspiration told the team what to avoid losing. It did not tell them what to win.

A winning aspiration closes those gaps. It names who you are trying to delight, what they need you to be better at than the alternative, and which alternatives you are competing against in the specific field where you have chosen to play. Those details are not decorative. Each one constrains a downstream choice: which capabilities to build, which field to invest in, which management system to reinforce.

The test is simple. Ask the aspiration a bad option. Find an opportunity that looks plausible but points in a different direction than the strategy. A winning aspiration can say no and explain why. A participation aspiration says yes, because it was not built to reject anything.

That asymmetry is the difference between a strategy and a wish. A wish accommodates. A strategy chooses.
breakdown.fullRead:
Most planning documents have an aspiration statement near the top. Most of them cannot name which customer they are trying to delight more than any other, which alternative that customer is choosing instead, or what the organization would need to do differently to beat that alternative for that specific person. The aspiration is broad by design. Everyone can see themselves in it. No one can lose anything by approving it.

An aspiration that cannot say no to anything is not making a choice. It is deferring one.

Think about what Saturn was asked to do. The aspiration was to give American car buyers a domestic alternative to the imports they were choosing. That sounds specific, but the import segment in the 1980s was not one thing: it was economy-conscious first-time buyers, reliability-seeking middle-income families, performance-seeking young professionals, and brand-curious urban drivers who had simply stopped trusting American quality. An alternative to imports named a competitive category, not a customer. And without naming a customer, Saturn could not name an advantage, because advantage is always relative to something: better than what, for whom, on which criteria?

The result was that Saturn had the investment of a real strategy and the direction of a participation aspiration. It invested heavily in a new plant, a new distribution model, a new dealer culture. Each of those investments was real. But without a specific winning aspiration naming which buyer to delight and which import to beat that buyer on, the investments did not compound. They each served the aspiration in parallel, not in sequence.

Consider what changes when the aspiration is specific. A hospital unit that names patients returning home after joint replacement surgery who need strong in-home support for the first thirty days has immediately said no to a different kind of aspiration: volume, speed, or broad surgical excellence. The specificity creates a constraint. That constraint is what makes the aspiration usable in a trade-off.

Here is the question worth asking about your own work: can the aspiration your team is working toward say no to a plausible option? Not a clearly wrong option, but a genuinely attractive one that points in a different direction. If it can, and the reason it says no is built into the aspiration itself, the aspiration is guiding strategy. If it cannot, the aspiration is occupying space that strategy needs to fill.

The problem is not that participation aspirations are dishonest. Most of them reflect genuine values. But values are not choices. A choice means that something else is not chosen. A participation aspiration is structured to avoid making that trade-off explicit, which means it cannot make it at all.

A winning aspiration is not more ambitious than a participation aspiration. It is more specific. That specificity is what turns an aspiration into the first choice of the strategic cascade: the one that shapes every other choice that follows.

Name the customer. Name the alternative. Ask whether your aspiration can say no. If the answer is not yet, that is where the next planning conversation needs to start.

examples.title: Margaux Cannot Choose Between Two Proposals
examples.scenario: You put two proposals on the table. One is a discharge follow-up call program: a nurse reaches out to post-surgical patients at 48 hours, seven days, and thirty days. The other is a patient room redesign: quieter lighting, adjustable beds, a dedicated family chair. Margaux's unit aspiration reads: be a leader in high-quality post-surgical care. Both proposals satisfy it without strain. She has one budget slot this cycle. The aspiration cannot help her choose.
examples.whatToDo: Name which patient the unit is specifically trying to serve better than the hospital in the next county. That choice will immediately distinguish between a follow-up program serving patients after discharge and a room design serving patients during admission. Without naming the specific patient and the specific alternative, the aspiration cannot adjudicate between two proposals both of which are defensible.
examples.whyItMatters: A winning aspiration is not the most comprehensive statement of a unit's values. It is the most specific statement of which patient it is committed to serving better than the available alternative. That specificity is what gives it the power to say no to a well-designed proposal.

examples.title: Marco's Support Queue Is Split and Going Nowhere
examples.scenario: Looking back on eight months of Monday support reviews, Marco could see the pattern that had made every roadmap negotiation a stalemate. Half the tickets were enterprise IT requests: slow to resolve, high value per client, requiring deep integrations his two-person team had never built. The other half were consumer onboarding questions: fast to answer, low retention rate, requiring a viral loop the team had never designed. The product aspiration said: the best productivity tool for teams who need flexible workflow management. Enterprise teams and consumer users both had workflows. The aspiration fit both without preferring either. The product could not move because the winning aspiration had never been named.
examples.whatToDo: Look at which customer type generates the highest percentage of revenue that would compound with additional investment, then rewrite the aspiration to name that customer and the specific alternative that customer is currently choosing instead. The rewritten aspiration should be able to say no to the next feature request from the other segment.
examples.whyItMatters: A founding aspiration that fits two incompatible customer types leaves the team renegotiating priorities between them with every build cycle. Naming one customer does not eliminate the other immediately; it makes every subsequent product and sales decision faster and more coherent.

examples.title: Hannah's Service Plan Has No Primary Customer
examples.scenario: At 10:15, Hannah presents the three-year service plan to the board. The vision statement covers the first slide: the library will be a welcoming, accessible resource for every member of our community. Fourteen programs are listed: story time, ESL classes, quiet study zones, extended Wi-Fi access, makerspace workshops, homebound delivery, and eight more. No audience is ranked. No competing library or digital platform is named as the alternative to beat. A board member asks which of those user groups the library is specifically trying to serve better than the library in the next county. Hannah has no answer ready. The aspiration says every member. The plan was built to serve that aspiration, not to say no to anything.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next service planning cycle, name the one or two user groups whose experience the library can realistically make better than the alternative they currently have access to. That answer will immediately reshape the program list, the staffing schedule, and the digital subscription budget.
examples.whyItMatters: An aspiration built to include everyone is built to require nothing specific. The first strategic choice the library must make is not which programs to add but which audience to delight more than the competing alternative in its region.

examples.title: David Stops Competing Against Everyone at Once
examples.scenario: The smell of garlic and olive oil at eleven-thirty in the morning, and the line cook is already behind. Before: David runs a family restaurant with forty-two items on the menu, decor that is neither casual nor elevated, and an aspiration to offer good food for everyone at a fair price. The fast-casual chain across the street has been open two months. The average check has dropped fourteen percent. He has lowered prices, added two lunch specials, and redesigned the loyalty card. Nothing has reversed the trend. After: he names a winning aspiration: the neighborhood's first-choice table for a weeknight dinner with kids. That sentence rejects the lunch battle with the fast-casual chain and the competition with the anniversary bistro two blocks over. Within sixty days he has cut the menu to twenty-eight items, dropped the loyalty card, and trained the servers on a different kind of greeting script.
examples.whatToDo: If you are competing against two different alternatives for two different types of customers, name which customer and which alternative matter more. Rewrite the aspiration to reflect that choice. The downstream changes to menu, pricing, and service model will follow once the aspiration can say no.
examples.whyItMatters: An aspiration of good food for everyone places a restaurant in competition with every other food option in the neighborhood simultaneously. The narrower aspiration does not serve fewer people; it makes the restaurant's choices coherent for the specific people it is trying to delight.

examples.title: Anya's Mixed Portfolio Wins Nothing
examples.scenario: 'Could I see a portfolio of similar brand work?' The commercial client's email arrived at 8:47 on a Thursday. Anya opened her portfolio site and saw the problem before she had scrolled past the first page. Wedding galleries and product photography shared the same homepage. A soft-focus ring shot was followed by a hard-lit skincare product on white. A candid ceremony moment was followed by a restaurant interior for a regional chain. Both were technically solid. Neither told a commercial client that Anya had built the referral network, the equipment setup, and the fast-turnaround editing system the work required. She had been taking both kinds of work for three years, telling herself the mixed portfolio showed range. The commercial client read it as someone who had not committed to either.
examples.whatToDo: Name the client type whose referral network would compound with each additional project. Then rebuild the portfolio to signal that specific aspiration: which work to show, which clients to quote, which projects to pursue next.
examples.whyItMatters: A mixed portfolio is a symptom of an unmade aspiration. It signals to each potential client type that someone else in the market has committed to serving them more specifically, because the work on screen does not.

examples.title: Ben Asks Why Either Crowd Would Drive Here
examples.scenario: The parks map is pinned to the back wall of the capital planning office, green patches scattered across the city grid. Two redesign proposals have been on Ben's desk for three weeks. The first: two synthetic turf fields and permanent scoreboards, designed for organized youth leagues. The second: a restored meadow, shaded picnic pavilions, and a nature play area for families. The department aspiration reads: create parks that serve the diverse recreational needs of all residents. Ben imagines a family in the northeast quadrant of the city on a Saturday morning, deciding whether to use this park or drive to the neighboring town's park. He realizes neither proposal gives that family a specific reason to stay here, because the aspiration has not named which residents the park is trying to delight more than the alternative a short drive away.
examples.whatToDo: Before choosing between the two proposals, name which user group the parks system is specifically competing for against the nearest alternative. That answer will indicate which proposal reinforces the winning aspiration and which one serves a different aspiration that has not been made explicit.
examples.whyItMatters: A park design that tries to serve organized leagues and unstructured families simultaneously serves neither as well as a design built for one. The aspiration question is not which design is better in the abstract; it is which design makes the right resident choose this park over the alternative.

questions.prompt: How does a winning aspiration differ from a participation aspiration?
choices: A winning aspiration names specific customers and specific alternatives to beat; a participation aspiration describes what to avoid losing without specifying either.

A winning aspiration requires a larger investment budget than a participation aspiration, because the precision needed to beat a specific competitor depends on the resources to outspend that competitor on the chosen battleground.

A winning aspiration is shorter and more memorable than a participation aspiration, since a concise statement is easier for employees to recall during daily decisions and therefore drives more consistent execution across the organization.
questions.explanation: The difference is specificity about customers and alternatives, not length, investment level, or ambition. A participation aspiration can be fully funded and genuinely held while remaining unable to guide a trade-off, because it does not name who to serve or what to beat them on.

questions.prompt: When a regional accounting firm writes this aspiration: 'Be the go-to partner for our clients' financial needs,' what diagnostic question best tests whether the aspiration can do strategic work?
choices: Does the aspiration use language clients already recognize?
Does the aspiration reflect the full range of services the firm currently offers?
Can the aspiration say no to adding a low-cost automated bookkeeping product for cost-sensitive clients?
questions.explanation: The can-it-say-no test checks whether an aspiration has enough specificity to reject a plausible option. If personalized service for small businesses can guide a decision about whether to add automated bookkeeping, it is working as a strategy. If it cannot say yes or no to that move, the specific customer and alternative have not been named clearly enough.

questions.prompt: The nonprofit community health clinic has the aspiration: 'Provide high-quality, accessible care to underserved patients in our region.' What is the most useful next step?
choices: Compare the two options by expected patient volume and fund the larger one, since serving more patients delivers more total impact and a clinic with limited resources should optimize for the population reached.
Rewrite the aspiration to name which patient type and which gap in existing care the clinic is most committed to closing.

Fund both at reduced capacity and track which one performs better over the year, because a staged comparison gives the board real-world evidence before committing the clinic's full capability investment to either direction.
questions.explanation: When an aspiration accepts both options equally, it is not specific enough to guide the choice. Comparing by volume is execution logic, not strategy. Funding both at reduced capacity splits resources without resolving the underlying strategic question of which patient to delight more than the alternative clinic in the region.

questions.prompt: Saturn's aspiration was to give American car buyers a domestic alternative to the imports they were choosing. Which specific gap made this a participation aspiration, not a winning one?
choices: The aspiration did not name which import buyers, which specific imports, or what advantage would make Saturn the better choice for a specific buyer.

The aspiration relied on national identity, not product quality, as the competitive frame, and patriotic positioning fades quickly once import brands invest in matching the build quality American buyers actually compare against.

The aspiration was set by GM corporate, not by the Saturn team itself, and corporate-imposed positioning rarely earns the deep operational commitment the brand team needed to keep the strategy intact through execution.
questions.explanation: Naming the import segment still left open which buyers within that segment to serve and what specific advantage would make them choose Saturn over the specific import they were already considering. Without those two specifics, Saturn's investments could not compound toward a clear advantage for any particular customer.

questions.prompt: When a coding bootcamp's aspiration reads: 'Help people transition into technology careers through immersive training,' what specific weakness does the aspiration carry into curriculum, marketing, and hiring decisions?
choices: Yes, because data analytics is adjacent to software engineering and the aspiration accepts both.
No, because the aspiration does not name which career transition or which employer relationships the bootcamp is trying to deepen.
Yes, because adding tracks increases enrollment and serves more people transitioning into technology.
questions.explanation: Help people transition into technology careers accepts data analytics, software engineering, UX design, cloud infrastructure, and dozens of other paths equally. Without naming the specific career transition and the employer relationship that makes graduates placeable, the aspiration cannot evaluate whether the data analytics offer fits the strategy.

questions.prompt: The community arts organization has the aspiration: 'Foster creativity and community engagement through accessible programming.' What does this aspiration fail to do as a strategic tool?
choices: The board has sound strategic judgment and can effectively serve multiple audiences simultaneously.
The aspiration has been tested and proved capable of guiding diverse program decisions.
The aspiration does not name a specific participant or outcome clearly enough to reject either program.
questions.explanation: An aspiration that approves both an after-school youth program and a professional exhibition series without forcing a trade-off is not guiding choices. It endorses anything consistent with creativity and community, which is nearly everything the organization might consider. The approval signals the aspiration is still playing to play.

questions.prompt: A freelance translator has built a client base across legal, medical, and marketing translation work. She writes a new aspiration: 'Deliver precise translations that preserve tone and meaning for clients who cannot afford mistranslation.' Which question best tests whether this is now a winning aspiration?
choices: Can the aspiration say no to a marketing translation client whose priorities differ from legal or medical precision standards?
Does the aspiration explain what motivated her to specialize in translation work?
Does the aspiration distinguish her from every other translator who also values precision?
questions.explanation: The cannot-afford-mistranslation language could describe legal, medical, and high-stakes marketing clients equally. The aspiration still does not name which client type to serve better than the alternative, so it cannot guide a decision between a legal document project and a product launch campaign that arrive on the same day.

questions.prompt: An independent bookshop rewrites its aspiration to 'be the community's source for books that spark meaningful conversation' and adds a book club, a curated staff picks shelf, and a local author event series. Eighteen months later all three programs are moderately used. What is the most useful strategic diagnosis?
choices: The aspiration was too narrow and should have been broadened to attract more segments, since a bookshop competing with a regional chain needs as many reasons to walk in the door as it can credibly offer.
The aspiration did not name which reader to serve better than the regional chain, so the three programs each pointed in a different direction rather than compounding.

The three programs are well-designed but the execution timeline was too short to show results, and a bookshop launching new community programs typically needs eighteen to twenty-four months before sustained customer behavior change becomes measurable.
questions.explanation: Books that spark meaningful conversation accepts book clubs, curated shelves, and author events as equally valid responses. Without naming which reader is choosing between the independent bookshop and the chain, and what specifically that reader needs the chain cannot provide, each program runs independently, not building a reinforcing advantage.

questions.prompt: Two B2B software aspirations are on the table. Aspiration A: 'Solve the data integration problem for mid-market companies.' Aspiration B: 'Be the data integration choice for mid-market companies that need enterprise-grade reliability without enterprise complexity, against alternatives that force a trade-off between the two.' Which is the stronger strategic aspiration, and why?
choices: Aspiration A, because it names the customer's specific problem instead of a competitive category, and starting from the customer's pain produces sharper product decisions than starting from a competitor comparison.

Neither; both are too narrow and will limit the company's total addressable market, since a B2B software company at this stage should keep the aspiration broad enough to support multiple growth paths as the product matures.
Aspiration B, because it names a specific customer, a performance standard that customer requires, and an implied alternative where errors are more acceptable.
questions.explanation: Aspiration B names the customer more specifically (teams that cannot afford errors in operational data), implies an alternative (less reliable platforms), and sets a performance standard that guides capability investment. Aspiration A names a job to be done without specifying what kind of team or what standard of performance constitutes winning for that team.

reviewCards.front: What two questions must a winning aspiration be able to answer?
reviewCards.back: Which specific customers are we trying to delight? And which specific alternatives are we trying to beat them on? An aspiration that cannot answer both concretely is still a participation aspiration.

reviewCards.front: What is the 'can it say no' test for a strategic aspiration?
reviewCards.back: Find a plausible, attractive option that points in a different direction than the strategy. If the aspiration can reject it and explain why, it is doing strategic work. If it cannot, the aspiration lacks the specificity to guide choices.

reviewCards.front: Why did Saturn's aspiration fall short as a winning aspiration?
reviewCards.back: It named what to avoid (losing import buyers) without naming which import buyers, which specific imports, or what advantage would make a Saturn buyer choose Saturn again. Without those specifics, investment could not compound toward a clear advantage.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between playing to win and playing to play?
reviewCards.back: Playing to win means naming a specific customer and a specific alternative to beat them on, with an aspiration specific enough to say no to a plausible option. Playing to play means describing what to avoid losing without specifying who to win for or what to win on.

reviewCards.front: Why does a broad aspiration fail to guide trade-off decisions?
reviewCards.back: An aspiration that accepts every option cannot reject any. Without the ability to say no, it cannot guide a choice between two plausible paths, which is the moment when strategic guidance is most needed.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to test a stated aspiration for strategic specificity by asking whether it can reject a plausible option. You practice naming the specific customer and the specific alternative the aspiration is designed to beat, and you use the can-it-say-no test to distinguish a winning aspiration from a participation aspiration in real planning situations.

ifThenPlans.context: choosing between two strategic directions
ifThenPlans.plan: If two investment options both fit the current aspiration equally well, the aspiration is not specific enough to guide the choice. Rewrite it to name the specific customer and the specific alternative before deciding.

ifThenPlans.context: writing a planning document or strategy deck
ifThenPlans.plan: Before finalizing the aspiration statement, run the can-it-say-no test: find a plausible option a competitor might pursue and ask whether your aspiration would accept or reject it. If it accepts, the aspiration is still playing to play.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a proposed new program or product
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask which specific customer the new program is trying to delight and which alternative that customer is currently choosing. If the aspiration cannot answer both questions, the program's strategic fit is undefined.

ifThenPlans.context: setting quarterly goals for a team
ifThenPlans.plan: Before setting goals, confirm the winning aspiration names both the customer and the alternative in one sentence. If the goals cannot be traced back to that sentence, each goal is running as a separate aspiration, not as part of a shared cascade.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find the aspiration for your project or team. Run the can-it-say-no test: identify one attractive option in your space that a competitor might pursue. Ask whether the aspiration accepts or rejects it. If it accepts without requiring any adjustment, write a revised aspiration that would allow it to say no to that specific option.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when a decision or resource allocation comes up, trace it back to the aspiration. Ask: does the winning aspiration prefer one option over the other? If the answer is no, the aspiration is not yet guiding that category of decision. Name the gap and decide whether to sharpen the aspiration or treat the decision as a new strategic choice.

memorableLines.text: Stefan was not choosing between good options. He was choosing between three options his aspiration had no basis for evaluating.
Saturn's aspiration told the team what to avoid losing. It did not tell them what to win.
An aspiration that cannot say no to anything is not making a choice. It is deferring one.

chapters.title: Where to Play
chapters.hook: Four channels, five customer segments, three geographies. Everything accessible. Nothing chosen. The field that results from saying yes to every opportunity is not a strategy; it is a list of places where the organization happens to be present.
chapters.counterintuition: Narrowing your competitive field is not a retreat. It is the action that makes all the resources you are already spending start to compound. In a field you did not choose, those resources are spread too thin to create any advantage. In a field you chose, they point in the same direction.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name one customer segment, channel, or geography you are currently serving that you did not consciously choose: it just accumulated. Ask what you would have to stop doing in that segment to compete better where you actually want to win. Write the answer down before the next decision meeting.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Where to play is not a description of where you currently operate. It is a set of explicit decisions about which customers, channels, and geographies you will compete for, and which you will stop serving or not enter.

breakdown.fastRead:
Rosa's grooming studio served dogs of all sizes, cats, rabbits, and the occasional exotic bird. The studio was optimized for nothing in particular. The appointment schedule mixed an hour-long doodle groom with a fifteen-minute rabbit trim with a two-hour Persian cat appointment that required a second groomer.

When a colleague asked which animals Rosa was actually best at grooming, the answer was immediate: companion dogs under fifteen pounds, city apartments, owners who booked monthly. She was not best at the others. She was just willing.

Rosa was not losing the bird clients. She was choosing not to keep them. That is what a field choice is.

Within a quarter of naming her field, the studio schedule had space for six more monthly dog clients. She had stopped competing in the cat and rabbit market where a dedicated competitor had better tools and shorter appointment times. She was winning in the field she had chosen, not spreading across the field she had inherited.
breakdown.deepRead:
The where-to-play choice operates on multiple dimensions simultaneously. A business that asks where should we compete is actually asking several questions at once: which customers, in which geographic area, through which channel, in which category, and at which vertical level of the value chain. Answering one and leaving the others open is not a complete field choice.

Bounty did not win by being everywhere. It won by concentrating where the advantage was real and the value could be captured. The premium segment of the paper towel shelf was not the largest segment; the value tier was. But the value tier was also the most competitive and the segment where the margin was thinnest. Choosing the premium segment allowed Bounty to build the capability and pricing position that a value-tier choice would have required them to sacrifice. The field choice made the how-to-win choice possible.

Every field that is not chosen is inherited. Inherited fields are the customers who found you first, the channels where you happened to win an early relationship, the geographies where it was convenient to be. They are not bad starting points. They are not a strategy.

The two field traps are the same trap from opposite directions: serving too many segments in the belief that breadth is safety, or staying in the segment you inherited because changing it feels like loss. In either case, the investment you are making cannot compound, because it is pointed at too many places or the wrong one.
breakdown.fullRead:
Field choice is the most neglected of the five cascade choices, for a simple reason: most organizations already occupy a field when they begin thinking about strategy. The customers exist. The channels are live. The geography is defined by where the sales team already has relationships. Asking the organization to reconsider the field means implying that the existing customers, channels, and geographies are somehow wrong, which is uncomfortable to say to the people who built them.

An inherited field is not the same as a chosen one. An inherited field means you compete in the places where you happen to be. A chosen field means you compete in the places where you have decided you can win.

Bounty is the cleaner illustration. The premium segment for paper towels was not the largest segment on the shelf; the value tier was larger. But the value tier was also the most competitive and the segment where margin was thinnest. Choosing the premium segment allowed Bounty to build the capability and pricing position that a value-tier choice would have forced them to sacrifice. The segment choice created the arena in which the advantage logic could be built and maintained.

Now think about a field you occupy that you did not actively select. It might be a customer type you started serving because they asked and you said yes. It might be a channel where you have presence because a partnership made it convenient. It might be a geography where one early client gave you a foothold that never turned into a deliberate expansion.

Ask this question: if you could redesign where you compete from scratch, knowing what you know now, would you choose that same customer, channel, and geography? If the answer is anything other than clearly yes, the field is worth reconsidering. Not immediately and not painlessly, but as a strategic question, not a historical fact.

The dimensions of the field choice that matter: which customers (segment, size, behavior, economics); which channels (direct, indirect, digital, physical); which geographies (local, regional, national, international); which categories (the product or service type you are selling within); and which vertical level (manufacturer, distributor, retailer, service layer). Each dimension is its own explicit decision. Leaving any of them at the default is leaving a piece of the field unchosen.

A field chosen across all five dimensions gives the how-to-win choice a specific arena. A field that is a collection of inherited defaults is an arena with no defined boundaries, where the organization competes against everyone for everyone and wins on nothing in particular.

Name your field. All of it. Customers, channels, geographies, categories, vertical scope. Then ask which of those dimensions you actually chose.

examples.title: Sophie Names the Channel She Can Actually Win
examples.scenario: 'We can get you into four hundred stores by Q3.' The buyer's offer sat in Sophie's inbox for three days. On one side of the spreadsheet: a grocery distribution deal, lower unit price, standardized packaging, a promotional budget the brand could not fund. On the other: eight hundred subscribers who paid full price every month and left product reviews without being asked. Sophie had built the subscriber list over two years by being available only through the brand's own site. The grocery deal would reach four hundred stores but require the brand to compete on a shelf where national players had lower costs and larger promotional budgets.
examples.whatToDo: Name the specific channel where the brand has a genuine advantage: the direct subscriber relationship and the full-price positioning it supports. Accepting the grocery deal means entering a channel where that advantage does not exist. Saying no to the grocery deal is not losing a channel; it is choosing the one where the brand can actually win.
examples.whyItMatters: A field choice is as much about which channels to leave as which to enter. A brand with a real advantage in one channel gives that advantage up the moment it enters a channel where the value equation is completely different.

examples.title: Andrew's Enrollment Data Shows Three Inherited Segments
examples.scenario: Three years of enrollment data told Andrew a story he had been avoiding. Adult beginners were canceling at twice the rate of other groups; he had been replacing them every quarter. Beginner children were the school's largest segment, but a competitor with a Suzuki-method program and a better parent waiting area had been winning that enrollment for two years. Advanced teens competed for spots in a university prep program that offered credentials the school could not match. By trying to serve all three segments, the school had become moderately adequate at each and genuinely strong at none.
examples.whatToDo: Look at which segment the current staff credentials, space configuration, and scheduling system actually support at a high level. Choose that segment explicitly and build the enrollment process, marketing, and program design around it. The other segments may continue on a limited basis, but they should not shape the infrastructure.
examples.whyItMatters: A music school that serves every age and skill level builds for no one in particular. The segment you choose should determine how the studio is scheduled, how teachers are hired, and what the student or parent experience is designed to achieve.

examples.title: Vincent's Referral Sheet Is Two Different Clinics
examples.scenario: At 7:45, Vincent reviews the referral sheet before the clinic opens. Twelve incoming patients this week: six from an orthopedic surgeon group whose referrals require insurance pre-authorizations, hospital-system coordination, and a billing process that takes ninety days to clear; six from a sports medicine network whose athletes need weekend availability, performance-targeted protocols, and a direct-pay model that closes in forty-eight hours. The clinic's equipment and floor layout were built for post-surgical recovery. The sports medicine referrals were being seen in the same space, on the same schedule, by the same therapists. Both groups were getting adequate care. Neither group was getting the clinic that had been built specifically for them.
examples.whatToDo: Map the referral channels, billing systems, scheduling requirements, and staff certifications that each patient segment requires. Then name which segment the clinic's current infrastructure supports at a competitive level. The other segment is an inherited field, not a chosen one.
examples.whyItMatters: Two referral channels that require different clinic identities cannot both be primary. Choosing one means the other becomes secondary, which may mean redirecting those referrals or building the separate infrastructure to serve both at a genuinely competitive level.

examples.title: Giulia's Distribution Map Shows Presence Without a Field
examples.scenario: Which of the two channels had the brand actually won a customer through from nothing, without a personal visit or a placement incentive? The investor's question caught Giulia mid-sentence. She had been describing the distribution plan: twenty-two on-premise restaurant and bar accounts, fourteen retail shelf slots across two regional chains. Every on-premise placement had required a personal visit, a tasting, and follow-up training with bar staff. Every retail placement was underperforming because the brand lacked the promotion budget to move product from shelf to basket. Both channels were live. Neither channel was winning on the brand's actual strengths. The investor was asking which channel the brand occupied versus which one the brand performed in.
examples.whatToDo: Track reorder rates and customer acquisition cost separately for each channel. The channel with the higher reorder rate and lower acquisition cost is the field the brand actually wins in. Name that as the primary field and build the sales team, inventory, and marketing around it.
examples.whyItMatters: Presence in two channels is not a field choice. A chosen field is where the brand's specific advantage: relationship depth, story, premium pricing, or occasion fit actually drives a repeat purchase without requiring a personal sales visit to make it happen.

examples.title: Tomasz Maps a Shifting Field Before He Picks One
examples.scenario: The scheduling board had three farm visits before 7 a.m. and a waiting room filling with companion animals at 8 a.m. Before: Tomasz ran a practice that said yes to every call. Farm visits, companion animals, the occasional wildlife rehabilitation referral. Each category required a different vehicle configuration, different medications, different hours, and different staff training. No category was being served at the level of a focused competitor. After: he mapped the geographic radius of each client type and found that the suburban fringe was growing at twelve percent per year while farm-visit demand had dropped twenty percent over the same period. The field was shifting beneath him. The practice had not yet chosen which direction to follow.
examples.whatToDo: Map the geographic trend for each patient segment over a three-year window. The segment growing faster in your geography is the field worth choosing explicitly. The field choice will then determine the equipment investment, the hiring plan, and the scheduling system.
examples.whyItMatters: A practice that serves two incompatible fields simultaneously cannot build the equipment, scheduling, or staff expertise that either field requires at a specialist level. The field choice is not about abandoning existing clients immediately; it is about naming which direction the infrastructure investment should point.

examples.title: Laura Discovers the Field She Already Won
examples.scenario: You are looking at a listener survey where you expected to find a general audience and found a profession instead. Laura had built a mid-size podcast about decision-making and leadership for two years, designing every episode for a thoughtful and curious listener who could be anyone. The survey showed something different: sixty-seven percent of respondents described themselves as working in operations management or supply chain. They had found the show not because of the broad framing but despite it, through a niche forum recommendation. The last ten episodes had been planned for the general-curiosity audience Laura hoped to reach. The actual audience was already there, in a specific field Laura had never explicitly chosen.
examples.whatToDo: Review the listener, customer, or user data for the field you are actually winning in without trying to. Name that field explicitly: which specific person has already chosen you, in which specific context, and for which specific reason. Then ask whether your content, positioning, or product is designed for that person or for someone broader.
examples.whyItMatters: An inherited audience is a field you have accidentally won. The question is whether it is the field worth competing in deliberately, and whether the current positioning is compounding that advantage or obscuring it.

questions.prompt: What does the where-to-play choice determine in a strategy cascade?
choices: The specific customers, channels, geographies, and categories in which the organization will and will not compete.
The advantage logic the organization will use to beat competitors in its current market.
The investment budget allocated to each growth initiative for the planning cycle.
questions.explanation: Where to play is the multi-dimensional field choice that shapes all subsequent cascade choices. It is distinct from how to win (advantage logic) and from budget allocation (which is an execution decision, not a strategic one). Leaving any field dimension at the default means leaving part of the strategic choice unmade.

questions.prompt: The regional accounting firm has been serving individual tax clients, small business clients, and mid-market clients for two decades. Partners feel stretched. What is the right strategic move?
choices: Continue serving all three client types but invest in a better scheduling system to handle volume more efficiently, since an operational fix would relieve the pressure on partner time without forcing a difficult capability decision.
Name which client type the firm's staff expertise, software systems, and referral network actually support at a competitive level, and build the firm's identity around that segment.

Add a fourth service line to diversify revenue and reduce dependence on any one client type, because broader offerings would protect the firm against demand swings in any single segment and stabilize annual revenue.
questions.explanation: Improving scheduling or adding services both leave the field undefined. Naming the client type to compete for explicitly forces decisions about the referral network, staff certifications, and pricing model. The other segments become secondary, not equal priorities, which is the difference between an inherited field and a chosen one.

questions.prompt: When a craft beverage brand is present in both on-premise (restaurant and bar) and off-premise (retail) channels without a clear advantage in either, what strategic problem does this configuration create?
choices: The brand needs a larger sales team to cover both channels more aggressively, since on-premise and off-premise each require dedicated relationship work and the current team is spread too thin to win in either.

The brand's product quality needs improvement before either channel can succeed, because the conversion gap in both channels suggests the underlying offer is not yet differentiated enough to earn shelf space or pour preference.
The brand occupies two channels without the specific advantage, pricing, or capability that either requires: present in both but winning in neither.
questions.explanation: Low reorder rates in both channels is not a quality or staffing problem; it is a field problem. Each channel requires a different advantage logic: on-premise requires relationship depth and occasion fit; off-premise requires promotional budget and shelf placement. A brand without the capability for either channel's requirements will underperform in both.

questions.prompt: If a specialty food brand sells through both direct-to-consumer subscription and grocery retail, with subscription generating eighty percent of margin from twenty percent of volume, what is the strategic implication?
choices: The brand should focus on improving grocery margins by negotiating better slotting terms with the retailer, since the grocery channel is too large to abandon and stronger terms would close the profitability gap with the subscription channel.
The brand has a genuine advantage in the subscription channel and is competing in the grocery channel without one, which will gradually drain the margin the subscription channel generates.

The brand has successfully diversified its distribution risk by serving two channels simultaneously, and the grocery channel's lower margin is acceptable as insurance against subscription churn in any given quarter.
questions.explanation: The margin gap between channels reveals a field mismatch. The subscription channel supports the brand's pricing, relationship, and storytelling advantage; the grocery channel does not. Continuing in a channel without an advantage consumes resources that could be reinforcing the channel where the advantage actually exists.

questions.prompt: When a music school serves beginner children, adult hobbyists, and advanced teens preparing for conservatory, and the advanced teens are leaving for competitor programs, what is the strategic move?
choices: Name advanced teens as the primary segment and redesign the scheduling, marketing, and teaching around what that specific segment requires.

Invest in additional staff credentials to improve quality across all three segments equally, since stronger faculty would lift outcomes for every segment and protect the school against any one segment's enrollment swings.

Reduce program offerings across all three segments to improve overall margin per student, because fewer programs would lower fixed costs and let the school stay viable across its current breadth of student types.
questions.explanation: Investing equally in all three segments is the inherited-field pattern: no segment gets chosen. Reducing offerings is a cost move, not a strategic one. Naming advanced teens as the chosen segment and building the infrastructure around their requirements creates a field choice with downstream implications for the how-to-win choice and the capabilities needed to deliver it.

questions.prompt: The rural veterinary practice serves both companion animals in a growing suburban edge and livestock in the surrounding farms. The owner is considering a major equipment purchase. What should come first?
choices: The practice should invest in livestock-visit capacity to serve an underserved rural market before a suburban competitor expands, since rural demand is steady and the practice already has the vehicles and field equipment to do this work.

The practice should hire a second veterinarian to handle both segments at a higher quality level, because the current capacity is the main constraint and additional staff would let the practice serve both segments without choosing.
The field is shifting: the practice has not yet chosen which direction to follow, and equipment investment, scheduling, and hiring decisions should wait until that choice is made.
questions.explanation: Adding capacity for the declining segment is investing in the wrong field. Adding staff without naming the field still leaves infrastructure pointing in two directions. The field shift makes the where-to-play choice urgent; the right next move is the choice itself, not the investment that would follow it.

questions.prompt: When a podcast host discovers that two-thirds of her listeners work in one specific professional field, but she has been designing the show for a general audience, what is the right strategic response?
choices: Name the professional audience as the chosen field, redesign content and positioning around that specific listener, and pursue advertising and partnership deals calibrated to that field.

Continue designing for the general-interest audience to avoid limiting total potential listeners, since the existing show is gaining listeners across topics and narrowing the framing would shrink the audience the host has already built.

Add a separate profession-specific episode series while keeping the general-interest framing for existing episodes, because a parallel series would test the demand without forcing a binary choice about the show's overall identity.
questions.explanation: The data reveals an inherited field: the show already wins in a specific professional segment without trying. Choosing that field explicitly allows content, positioning, and monetization to compound. Keeping the general framing while adding a separate series leaves the field unchosen and splits the audience without building advantage in either direction.

questions.prompt: Bounty concentrated on the premium segment of the paper towel market instead of competing across the full shelf. Which strategic logic does this illustrate?
choices: Bounty's success was primarily driven by premium-segment buyers being less sensitive to private-label competition, which makes share easier to defend during retailer price pressure than in the value segment where store brands dominate.
Choosing one segment let Bounty build the pricing and positioning to win there; competing across the full shelf would have made that impossible to sustain.

Bounty's success was primarily driven by product quality, not by field choice, since stronger absorbency and durability would have won the market in any segment and the premium positioning was an artifact of the higher price point.
questions.explanation: The Bounty case illustrates that field choice enables the how-to-win choice that follows it.
