Competing across the full shelf would have required Bounty to match the value tier's pricing while also maintaining a premium position, which is unsustainable. The segment choice created the arena in which the advantage logic could be built and maintained.

questions.prompt: The physical therapy clinic serves two referral channels: orthopedic surgeons (high-value, short-duration cases) and primary care doctors (lower-value, longer-duration cases). The clinic owner is considering improvements. What is the right strategic move?
choices: Option A, because improving billing efficiency is measurable and reduces a concrete operational drag, giving the clinic free cash flow to invest in whichever field choice it eventually makes.

Both options equally, because they target different parts of the same underlying problem and addressing operational friction in parallel with strategic positioning produces the most balanced improvement.
Option B: naming the field first is the strategic choice; billing efficiency is an operational fix within a field the clinic has not yet chosen to be in.
questions.explanation: Option A improves execution within an unchosen field. Option B makes the field choice that determines what operational improvements should follow. A billing improvement in the wrong field is still investment in the wrong field. The sequence matters: choose the field, then optimize the operations within it.

reviewCards.front: What are the five dimensions of a complete where-to-play choice?
reviewCards.back: Which customers (segment, size, behavior, economics); which channels (direct, indirect, digital, physical); which geographies (local, regional, national, international); which categories (product or service type); and which vertical level of the value chain. Each dimension requires an explicit decision.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between an inherited field and a chosen field?
reviewCards.back: An inherited field is where you currently operate by default: the customers who found you first, the channels that were convenient, the geographies where early relationships formed. A chosen field is where you have decided to compete because you can win there. Only the chosen field can be consistently won.

reviewCards.front: What did Bounty illustrate about where-to-play choices?
reviewCards.back: Bounty concentrated on the premium segment, bypassing the full shelf competition. This allowed Bounty to build the pricing and capability required to win in that specific arena, which would have been unsustainable while also competing in the value tier. The field choice made the how-to-win choice possible.

reviewCards.front: What does a brand lose by serving two incompatible channel types simultaneously?
reviewCards.back: Each channel requires different advantage logic, pricing, and capabilities. A brand present in both without the specific resources for either underperforms in both. Investment cannot compound toward advantage in either channel.

reviewCards.front: What question tests whether a field choice is explicit or still a default?
reviewCards.back: Ask: if you could redesign your competitive field from scratch, knowing what you know now, would you choose the same customers, channels, and geographies? If the answer is anything other than clearly yes, the field is worth reconsidering, not accepting as a fixed fact.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish a chosen field from an inherited one by tracing how each customer segment, channel, or geography was added. You practice naming the specific dimensions of the where-to-play choice (customers, channels, geography, category, vertical scope) and use the inherited-versus-chosen test to identify which dimensions are still at the default.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a new distribution or sales channel opportunity
ifThenPlans.plan: Before saying yes to a new channel, ask whether the brand or practice has the specific advantage required to win in that channel. A channel that requires capabilities you do not have is not a field extension; it is a second field that will drain resources from the first.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a product or service portfolio
ifThenPlans.plan: For each customer segment or category in the portfolio, trace when and how it was added. If it was added because the opportunity was convenient, not because it fit the chosen field, name it as an inherited segment and evaluate whether it belongs in the field choice going forward.

ifThenPlans.context: planning hiring or infrastructure investment
ifThenPlans.plan: Before hiring for a new capability or building new infrastructure, confirm that the investment is required by the chosen field. An investment that serves an inherited segment may be spending resources in the wrong arena.

ifThenPlans.context: deciding whether to exit a segment or channel
ifThenPlans.plan: If exiting a segment or channel is under consideration, test whether that segment or channel was ever explicitly chosen. If it was inherited rather than chosen, exiting it is not a loss; it is completing the field choice that was never made.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one segment, channel, or geography you are currently serving that was never explicitly chosen. Write down when and how you started serving it. Ask whether, if you were designing the field from scratch today, you would choose it. If not, name one concrete action you could take to reduce your investment there.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, when a new opportunity, partnership, or customer request comes up, ask whether it fits the field you have chosen or whether it is a new field in disguise. Name it explicitly before deciding. Opportunities that require different customers, channels, or capabilities are not extensions of the current field; they are separate strategic choices that should be evaluated as such.

memorableLines.text: Rosa was not losing the bird clients. She was choosing not to keep them. That is what a field choice is.
Bounty did not win by being everywhere. It won by concentrating where the advantage was real and the value could be captured.

An inherited field is not the same as a chosen one. An inherited field means you compete in the places where you happen to be. A chosen field means you compete in the places where you have decided you can win.

chapters.title: How to Win
chapters.hook: After three years of closing gaps, every metric matched the market leader. Market share had not moved. Matching is not beating.
chapters.counterintuition: Being better at what the competitor already does is not the same as finding a different win path. The advantage logic that makes a competitor strong in its chosen field is exactly what makes it hard to beat on those same terms. The question is not how to be better at their game, but which problem you are able to solve differently.
chapters.tryThisNow: Name the strongest thing your closest competitor does. Now ask: are you currently trying to beat them at that same thing, or are you solving a problem they are not even optimizing for? Write down the problem you could own that they are structurally unable to own without becoming something different.
chapters.keyTakeaway: The how-to-win choice names which problem you will solve differently and what value equation makes you the better choice for that specific customer.

breakdown.fastRead:
Nora's tutoring center competed against the regional franchise with forty subjects, online scheduling, and standardized curricula available in twelve locations. She had been responding by adding subjects, building a website, and standardizing her session formats to look more systematic.

She was not closing the gap. She was entering the game the franchise had already won.

Nora stopped trying to match the franchise's coverage. She started doing the one thing the franchise could not: remember what confused each student last Tuesday.

The franchise ran a session and moved on. Its model required it. Nora's model could track the exact concept that stopped a student three weeks ago and approach it from a different angle this week. Parents began calling not because she was cheaper or broader but because their child had stopped dreading the next session. That is a value equation the franchise did not have and could not build without becoming something other than a franchise.
breakdown.deepRead:
The how-to-win choice is not a quality target. It is a decision about what kind of problem you are going to solve better than the alternative and which problem you are going to leave to them.

Head-to-head competition means choosing the same terms the competitor is strongest at: lower price, faster response, better ratings on the same dimensions the competitor already dominates. The competitor can match and extend any improvement you make on those terms, because they have already invested more in exactly that capability. Improving faster is not a strategy; it is a race you started later.

An alternate win path starts with a different question: which problem is the competitor not optimizing for?

Glad ForceFlex did not win by making a cheaper bag or fitting more bags in the box. It won by solving a failure mode the competitor had not named. Bag strength under heavy load was not what the established competitors' marketing optimized for or what their manufacturing processes were designed to improve. The ForceFlex value equation was a bag that does not fail when it matters: a different game entirely, and one the competitor could not immediately copy without changing its own offer logic.

The distinction matters because it determines where investment compounds. In a head-to-head game, every improvement is visible to the competitor and invites a matching response. In an alternate-path game, the improvement addresses a problem the competitor has not yet named, which means the competitor may not respond for long enough for the advantage to establish itself.
breakdown.fullRead:
Think about the last time you improved something about your product or service in direct response to a competitor's move. You reduced a price they had lowered. You added a feature they had launched. You sped up a process they had streamlined. The improvement was real. The gap it was designed to close probably still exists.

The question is not how to be better at what the competitor already does. The question is which problem the competitor is structurally unable to solve without becoming something different.

That question points in a different direction than the standard competitive analysis. It is not asking about the competitor's current weaknesses; it is asking about the problems the competitor's strengths require them to ignore. A competitor optimized for throughput cannot optimize simultaneously for depth per interaction. A competitor built for scale cannot build simultaneously for the kind of local knowledge that only accumulates over time in one specific place. The structural requirements of the competitor's model create blind spots, and those blind spots are where the alternate win path lives.

Glad ForceFlex found the blind spot in the trash-bag market. The established competitors were optimizing for price per unit and count per box: the most visible purchase criteria on the shelf. Bag strength under load was the problem the market had accepted as inherent to the product category. ForceFlex made it an advantage instead. Competing on bag count or price would have required ForceFlex to beat competitors who had already built their entire manufacturing and marketing logic around those criteria. Competing on strength required building a different manufacturing approach and naming a different value equation.

Now apply this to your own situation. Name the two or three dimensions your strongest competitor is currently optimizing for. Then ask: what does their optimization on those dimensions require them to leave unsolved? A speed-focused competitor leaves depth unsolved. A price-focused competitor leaves trust unsolved. A breadth-focused competitor leaves specificity unsolved. The unsolved problem your customer experiences regularly is where the alternate win path starts.

The test for whether an advantage route is genuinely alternate is whether the competitor can match it without changing what they fundamentally are. A modular addition, a new hire, or a pricing adjustment can be copied quickly. A value equation built around a capability that requires a different operating model, a different customer relationship, or a different kind of knowledge takes much longer to copy, and harder to copy is where durable advantage lives.

That test is not just retrospective. Apply it to the investment you are considering now. Ask whether the competitor can match it without restructuring the parts of their business that give them their current advantage. If they can, the investment is an improvement to a contested game. If they cannot, the investment is a path to a different one.

examples.title: Grace Finds the One Client Who Did Not Leave
examples.scenario: Grace traced the last five clients who had left the firm. Four of them had moved to a national practice for faster digital filing: the national firm's processing time was forty-eight hours and the firm's was ten days. She had been investing in software to close that gap. The fifth client had stayed, and had sent two referral notes with him. She pulled the file and read the referral letter: 'They caught something the software flagged as standard that our previous firm knew was a regulatory exception in our sector.' The departing clients had wanted speed. The staying client had wanted judgment. The firm had been competing on the wrong dimension entirely.
examples.whatToDo: Name the specific capability the national firm cannot deliver at scale: industry-specific knowledge that catches what automated filing cannot flag. Build the practice around that capability and price accordingly. Stop competing on processing speed.
examples.whyItMatters: An accounting practice that competes on software speed enters a race the software vendor already won. The alternate win path is the value the national firm structurally cannot deliver: judgment developed in one specific industry context that no automation replaces.

examples.title: Daniel Chooses a Different Game Than the Academy
examples.scenario: You are in a room full of parents whose older children played for the regional academy and transferred out mid-season. They are sitting in plastic chairs waiting for Daniel to explain why this club is worth joining. His first instinct is to say: we will get your child recruited. That sentence puts the club in direct competition with the academy's credential, travel tournament record, and coaching staff, all of which are stronger. Daniel stops before he says it. The academy's recruiting model has a requirement: it serves players worth recruiting and moves on from those who are not. The club has no such requirement. That is not a weakness. It is a different value equation.
examples.whatToDo: Name the outcome the academy cannot offer without becoming a different organization: consistent development, no cutoff for players who develop slowly, a path that does not require a recruiting result to justify the investment. Present that as the value equation, not as a consolation prize for families who could not make the academy.
examples.whyItMatters: A club that competes on recruitment outcomes enters head-to-head competition with an academy that has invested everything in exactly that outcome. The alternate win path is built on the player need the academy's model structurally cannot serve: long-term development without the pressure of a recruitment timeline.

examples.title: Henrik Stops Timing His Pour and Starts Remembering Names
examples.scenario: The espresso machine steams at 6:55 in the morning and the queue already reaches the door. Before: Henrik has taped a stopwatch comparison above the register: his shop, four minutes average to door; the chain across the street, ninety seconds. He hired a second barista for peak hours to close the gap. Costs rose. Margins shrank. Morning traffic stayed flat. After: he removed the stopwatch and spent two weeks writing down regulars' orders from memory. By the third week he was calling the order before the customer reached the counter. The chain's format optimized for throughput and could not do that without changing the entire operating model. Henrik's shop became the destination for the customer the chain's speed had no room for.
examples.whatToDo: Identify the specific customer behavior that the chain's format cannot accommodate: the regular who wants to be remembered, the customer who wants to ask a question about the origin of the beans, the person who wants the experience of being known. Build the value equation and operational model around that customer.
examples.whyItMatters: A four-minute pour time is not a competitive advantage over ninety seconds. The question for Henrik was never how to close the speed gap but which problem the chain's speed creates that he can solve instead.

examples.title: Chiara's Nurse Names the Alternate Win Path
examples.scenario: At 8:30, Chiara presents the two options to the staff before the first patient. Option one: expand weekend hours to match the urgent care chain's coverage. Option two: extend weekday appointment slots from thirty to sixty minutes and reduce the daily patient count. A nurse at the back of the room says: 'The urgent care will always have more hours. What they will never have is an hour.' The room is quiet. The urgent care chain's model is built around high visit volume. Adding time per visit would require restructuring the billing model, the staffing ratio, and the patient flow system. The clinic can do what the chain cannot without becoming something other than an urgent care chain.
examples.whatToDo: Invest in the longer appointment time and build the clinical model around the specific patient need that an hour makes possible: chronic condition management, patient history continuity, follow-up that fits within one session. Name that as the value equation the clinic offers, not framing it as a limitation on visit volume.
examples.whyItMatters: A clinic competing on coverage hours will always lose to a chain with more locations and more funding. The alternate win path is the value equation the chain has no incentive to build: depth of care per visit that only exists when time is not the main cost being managed.

examples.title: Kasia Asks Whether the Coffee Bar Is an Alternate Path or a Me-Too Move
examples.scenario: 'The coffee brings people in. Once they are in, they buy books.' Kasia's retail advisor had a point. She had been losing online price comparisons for three years. The advisor was right that foot traffic was the problem. He had drawn a floor plan with a circled corner and written coffee bar option. Kasia looked at the chain coffee shop on the same block that was doing four times her volume. She asked: 'Will anyone walk past that to buy a latte from a bookshop?' The advisor paused. She continued: 'But would they walk past it to have a staff member who has read every book in the store and can tell you in ninety seconds which one is exactly right for the trip you just described?' That was not a coffee bar. That was a different value equation.
examples.whatToDo: Invest in the staff capability that the platform structurally cannot deliver: staff who have read each title personally and can route a browser to exactly the right one in under ninety seconds based on a brief conversation. Build the marketing around that capability, not around the square footage or the coffee menu.
examples.whyItMatters: A coffee bar competes on a dimension where chain coffee shops have more scale, more experience, and more brand. The alternate win path is the one thing an online platform's algorithm cannot replicate: a human who has read each title and can match exactly the right one to this specific customer standing here today.

examples.title: Chris Finds the Advantage the Program Never Named
examples.scenario: Chris reviewed five years of placement data from the apprenticeship's top employer. Every graduate hired in the first hiring round, across five cohorts, had the same characteristic: they had worked on live production systems for twelve months before graduation. University graduates from the same employer's recruitment pipeline took an average of six months of internal retraining before reaching the same productivity level. Chris had been positioning the apprenticeship as a faster route to the same credential. The credential was never what the employer was paying for. The employer was paying for twelve months of live system experience compressed into two years. That was the value equation. The program had never claimed it.
examples.whatToDo: Name the specific advantage in employer terms: a graduate who reaches full production readiness in weeks, not months, because they have been working on real systems since day one. Stop competing on credential comparison. Lead with readiness and build the curriculum framing, alumni testimonials, and employer partnerships around that specific outcome.
examples.whyItMatters: A program that competes on credentials enters head-to-head competition with a degree program that will always have more academic depth. The alternate win path is the one thing the degree cannot deliver without becoming an apprenticeship: time on live systems before graduation.

questions.prompt: How does head-to-head competition differ from choosing an alternate-path value equation?
choices: Head-to-head means competing on the same terms the competitor is already strongest at; an alternate path means solving a problem the competitor is not optimizing for.

Head-to-head means competing on price; an alternate path means competing on a premium offer, because the price-versus-premium axis is the primary dimension on which most competitive positions are differentiated.

Head-to-head means targeting the same customer; an alternate path means targeting a different customer segment, and the choice of which customer to serve is the foundation of every strategic position.
questions.explanation: The distinction is in the problem being solved, not the customer or price point. Head-to-head competition uses the same terms the competitor has already optimized for. An alternate path identifies a problem the competitor is not optimizing for and builds a value equation around solving it differently.

questions.prompt: When a regional accounting firm is losing clients to a national firm offering faster processing and lower fees, what is the strategically correct response?
choices: Invest in the same tax software the national firm uses to match their processing speed, since closing the technology gap removes the most visible reason clients are leaving and buys time to rebuild the relationship.
Name the value the national firm cannot offer at scale (industry-specific judgment that catches what automation misses) and build the practice around that capability.

Lower the hourly rate by twenty percent to reduce the price gap with the national firm, because price is the most actionable lever available and a temporary rate cut can stop client attrition while a longer-term plan develops.
questions.explanation: Matching the software or lowering the rate keeps the firm in head-to-head competition on dimensions the national firm has already optimized. The alternate path names the value the national firm cannot deliver at scale: the judgment that accumulates from years of work in a specific industry and cannot be automated.

questions.prompt: The specialty coffee shop is competing against a chain location with ninety-second service times, loyalty rewards, and prices fifteen percent below the shop's. The owner is considering speed improvements and a loyalty program. What is the strategic objection?
choices: The owner has correctly identified the main source of the chain's advantage and is addressing it directly.
The owner needs to decide between competing on speed and competing on quality before making the hiring decision.
The owner is competing on the chain's strongest terms, which the chain can sustain and extend more easily than the shop can.
questions.explanation: The chain's speed advantage is structural: it was built for high throughput and can sustain any speed improvement the shop makes by investing further. Adding a barista temporarily closes a gap the chain can reopen. The alternate path is a value equation built around something the chain structurally cannot offer: knowing regulars, being a destination, not a throughput stop.

questions.prompt: Glad ForceFlex chose not to compete on price or bag count in the trash-bag market. What strategic logic drove that choice?
choices: Price and bag count were the competitors' strongest terms; competing there required matching an advantage the competitor could sustain and extend more easily.

Price and bag count were not significant factors in the trash-bag purchase decision at that time, and the leader's marketing emphasis on these dimensions was actually misreading what customers were responding to at the shelf.
ForceFlex's proprietary stretch-film process required higher per-unit costs that made matching competitor prices structurally unprofitable at the volumes Glad needed to achieve in mass retail.
questions.explanation: The ForceFlex case illustrates that competing on the competitor's strongest terms means fighting in an arena the competitor has already optimized. The alternate win path (bag strength under heavy load) addressed a problem rivals were not optimizing for, which created a different game the competitor could not immediately copy.

questions.prompt: The trade apprenticeship program has been losing candidates to four-year engineering degree programs. The director is considering adding coursework to match the academic prestige. What is the strategic objection?
choices: Academic content is too expensive to add within the current grant budget without restructuring the program's hands-on curriculum hours.
Candidates who prefer academic coursework over hands-on system experience are generally better served by the university degree pathway.
Adding academic coursework enters the same competition the degree program already wins; the alternate path is what only the apprenticeship delivers: production-system readiness before graduation.
questions.explanation: Adding academic content puts the apprenticeship in direct competition on the degree program's strongest terms. The genuine alternate value equation is already visible in the placement data: employers get graduates who reach full productivity faster because they have been working on live systems throughout the program, something a degree cannot provide without becoming an apprenticeship.

questions.prompt: The youth soccer club is losing players to a regional academy with elite coaching credentials and tournament access. The club director is considering matching academy investment. What is the strategic alternative?
choices: Hire a credentialed former professional coach to match the academy's coaching level, since coaching quality is the most visible differentiator parents compare and closing that gap removes the academy's biggest recruiting advantage.
Name a value equation the academy cannot offer without becoming something different: consistent development, no cutoff at a recruiting milestone, a path for every player.

Offer a lower monthly fee to attract budget-conscious families who cannot afford the academy, because price is the most actionable lever available and a stable budget tier captures the families the academy structurally cannot reach.
questions.explanation: Matching the coach credential or lowering price keeps the club in head-to-head competition on terms the academy has already won. The alternate path is built on the player need the academy's elite-recruitment model structurally cannot serve: long-term development without the pressure of a recruitment timeline that the academy's business model requires.

questions.prompt: When a community health clinic is deciding whether to match an urgent care chain's walk-in availability and price transparency, what diagnostic question should determine the choice?
choices: Ask which option requires the urgent care chain to change its fundamental operating model to match; the thing the chain cannot copy is where the alternate win path lives.

Ask which option can be launched fastest and measure patient response after three months, since speed-to-market lets the clinic test directional bets without committing the entire capital budget to a single option upfront.

Ask which option the clinic's current staff prefers and implement that one first, because staff buy-in is the largest predictor of execution quality and a preferred option will produce stronger initial results regardless of strategic logic.
questions.explanation: The chain can always add more hours by adding more locations and staff. It cannot add more time per visit without restructuring its billing model and patient flow system. The alternate win path is the option the competitor cannot copy without becoming something fundamentally different. Speed of launch and staff preference are execution criteria, not strategic ones.

questions.prompt: The regional accounting firm names its alternate advantage as industry-specific judgment. Two years later, the national competitor announces a modular add-on offering 'industry insights.' Should the regional firm change strategy?
choices: The national competitor has now closed the gap, so the regional firm should return to competing on processing speed, since the basis of differentiation has been neutralized and the firm must defend the dimension where clients are now comparing.
Alternate win paths remain durable only when the competitor cannot match them without fundamentally changing their operating model; a modular add-on is not the same as the underlying capability.

The national competitor's response proves the regional firm overestimated the value of its advantage, and the firm should investigate which other dimensions the competitor's product investments suggest are the real client priorities.
questions.explanation: A competitor can add a process step without building the underlying judgment that makes the step effective. The durability of an alternate path depends on whether the competitor can replicate the capability, not just the activity. An automated review step added to a volume-processing firm is not the same as the knowledge that develops over years of work in a specific industry.

questions.prompt: The independent bookshop is considering two options: Option A, add a coffee bar; Option B, invest in staff expertise and curated recommendation. Which is the stronger strategic option, and why?
choices: Option A, because foot traffic is the fundamental driver of sales in a physical retail business, and a coffee bar provides the dwell-time and cross-traffic that the bookshop's existing layout cannot generate on its own.

Both equally: the coffee bar brings customers in and the staff training converts them, and the two investments compound by combining traffic generation with conversion improvement to lift the bookshop on both dimensions at once.
Option B, because staff expertise cannot be replicated online, while a coffee bar puts the bookshop in direct competition with chains that already do it better.
questions.explanation: A coffee bar adds a service that a nearby chain coffee shop already provides with more scale and experience. Expert staff recommendation is a capability the algorithm cannot deliver, which is a genuine alternate path. The test for any proposed investment: can the competitor match it without changing what they fundamentally are? The coffee competitor can. The online platform cannot.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between head-to-head competition and an alternate-path value equation?
reviewCards.back: Head-to-head means competing on the same terms the competitor is already strongest at. An alternate path means identifying a problem the competitor is not optimizing for and building a value equation around solving it differently.

reviewCards.front: What question identifies an alternate win path?
reviewCards.back: Which problem is the competitor not optimizing for? The problem the competitor ignores or cannot solve without changing what it fundamentally is creates the space for a different value equation.

reviewCards.front: What did Glad ForceFlex illustrate about the how-to-win choice?
reviewCards.back: Rather than competing on price or bag count, ForceFlex solved a problem rivals were not optimizing for: bag strength under heavy load. The value equation was a bag that does not fail when it matters, which created a different game the competitor could not immediately copy.

reviewCards.front: What is the structural problem with matching a stronger competitor on their own strongest terms?
reviewCards.back: A competitor who has invested longest and heaviest in their strongest area can sustain and extend that advantage more easily than a challenger can close it. Competing on those terms means catching up to a moving target on terrain the competitor chose and designed for themselves.

reviewCards.front: What test distinguishes a genuine alternate win path from a better-version-of-the-same offer?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the competitor can match the approach without fundamentally changing their operating model. If they can add it as a module or hire for it easily, it is a better-same offer. If matching it requires them to become something different, it is an alternate path.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to identify whether a proposed competitive move is head-to-head or alternate-path by asking which problem the competitor is not optimizing for. You practice applying the structural-copy test to distinguish a genuine alternate win path from an improvement on the competitor's own strongest terms.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a competitive proposal or new service launch
ifThenPlans.plan: Before approving it, ask which competitive dimension it targets and whether the strongest competitor in the field has already optimized for that dimension. A proposal that competes on the competitor's strongest terms requires a reason the competitor cannot simply match it.

ifThenPlans.context: responding to a market leader extending their advantage
ifThenPlans.plan: Instead of matching the extension, identify the failure mode the market leader's move makes worse or ignores. The space the leader cannot serve without changing their model is where the alternate path lives.

ifThenPlans.context: when customers leave for a stronger competitor
ifThenPlans.plan: Trace whether the departing customers left because the competitor was better at what both were trying to do, or because the competitor offered something you were not competing on at all. The second pattern is a signal that the how-to-win choice needs to change, not just the execution quality.

ifThenPlans.context: when pricing pressure makes margins unsustainable
ifThenPlans.plan: Price pressure is usually a symptom of head-to-head competition on the same value equation as the market. Ask whether there is a problem the competitor is not optimizing for that would command a different price from the customer who needs it solved.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name the one thing your closest competitor does that you have been trying to match or beat. Write down what it would take for you to win on that specific dimension. Then ask: what is a problem in your customer's experience that the competitor has not yet named as something worth solving? That is where the alternate win path starts.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: When a customer makes a request or a complaint, note whether it points toward something the competitor is already solving well or something the competitor has not addressed. Complaints the competitor is also getting are execution problems. Complaints the competitor is not getting could be the beginning of a different value equation.

memorableLines.text: Nora stopped trying to match the franchise's coverage. She started doing the one thing the franchise could not: remember what confused each student last Tuesday.
Glad ForceFlex did not win by making a cheaper bag or fitting more bags in the box. It won by solving a failure mode the competitor had not named.
The question is not how to be better at what the competitor already does. The question is which problem the competitor is structurally unable to solve without becoming something different.

chapters.title: Play to Your Strengths
chapters.hook: Fourteen capabilities in the review, three required by the strategy. The other eleven were why the three never built actual advantage.
chapters.counterintuition: Most organizations find they have more capabilities than their strategy needs. That abundance is the warning sign. A capability that does not connect to the how-to-win choice consumes investment without compounding toward any advantage.
chapters.tryThisNow: State your current how-to-win choice in one sentence. Then name the three specific things your organization must be able to do well for that choice to work. For each one, rate honestly: have it, building it, or not yet exists. The gap is where the investment belongs: not at the top of a strengths list.
chapters.keyTakeaway: The capability audit runs backward from the how-to-win choice: what must the strategy require, not what the organization currently does well.

breakdown.fastRead:
Leon ran a landscape architecture firm with genuine skill in four areas: ecological restoration, residential garden design, commercial plaza work, and public park planning. Each area was real. His business development presentation listed all four.

He landed no significant work for six months.

When he traced where the firm's strongest projects had come from, the answer was specific: complex ecological restoration for land trusts and conservation organizations. Those clients needed scientific knowledge, community engagement, and regulatory navigation that most design firms could not provide together. The other three areas were solid. They were not the system that made the firm irreplaceable.

Leon was not weak in the other three areas. He was diluting the one area that made the firm irreplaceable.

He rebuilt the presentation around the capability system the ecological work required. The next three pitches were won against firms that offered broader services.
breakdown.deepRead:
A capability system is the set of specific things an organization must be able to do well for its how-to-win choice to deliver a genuine advantage. It is not a list of what the organization currently does. It is what the strategy requires.

The distinction matters because the how-to-win choice sets the direction first. The capability audit runs backward from it. The question is not which strengths are impressive or historically significant; the question is which capabilities are required to deliver the advantage the strategy has chosen to build.

Gillette fit because the things Gillette was able to do well were the specific things P&G's strategy needed done. Precision manufacturing, deep consumer insight, and global distribution capabilities reinforced P&G's how-to-win choices in a specific set of consumer categories. The acquisition was not justified by Gillette's market position or brand value alone; it was justified by capability fit. What Gillette could do well was what P&G's strategy required to be done well.

An isolated strength that does not connect to the how-to-win choice is not a strategic advantage. It is a cost. The organization must invest to maintain it, and the investment does not compound toward the advantage the strategy is trying to build.

The backward-mapping question is: what would the organization need to be able to do, specifically and at a high level, for the how-to-win choice to work? The answer defines the required capability system. Checking honestly whether that system exists, is under construction, or has not yet been started is the capability audit that matters.
breakdown.fullRead:
Most capability conversations start from what the organization already has: a list of things it does well, accumulated over time, organized by department or function. The question is then how to use those strengths to build strategy. But that sequence produces a strategy shaped by what exists, not a capability system built for what the strategy requires.

Starting from the how-to-win choice runs in the opposite direction. The question is not what can we do with what we have, but what must we be able to do well for this specific advantage to work in this specific field? That question produces a different answer, and the answer often includes capabilities the organization does not yet have.

What makes a capability system different from a list of strengths is that the required capabilities reinforce each other. A strength that operates in isolation is useful but not compounding. A capability system is a set of activities where each one makes the others more effective. A firm that builds deep industry knowledge develops the regulatory familiarity that accelerates client trust, which generates the referral network that brings in the next case, which adds another layer of industry pattern-recognition. The activities support each other. Remove any one, and the others work less well. That is the difference between a list and a system.

Gillette illustrated what capability fit looks like when the backward mapping is done right. P&G did not acquire Gillette because the brand was large or the market position was strong. P&G acquired Gillette because Gillette's capability system reinforced what P&G's strategy needed done. The fit was in the activities, not in the revenue size or brand recognition, which were real but secondary to the strategic question.

An isolated strength that does not connect to the how-to-win choice creates cost, not advantage. The organization must fund it, staff it, and maintain it, and none of that investment compounds toward the advantage the cascade is trying to build.

Now apply the backward-mapping question to your own situation. Name your current how-to-win choice. Then list the three things your organization would need to do exceptionally well for that choice to produce a genuine advantage in the field you have chosen. Check each one honestly: does the capability exist at the required level, is it under construction, or does it not yet exist? The gap between what the strategy requires and what the capability system can currently deliver is where the investment question belongs.

The capability audit is not a performance review. It is a strategic question: does the activity system we currently have point in the direction the how-to-win choice requires? If it does not, the gap is a strategic decision, not an operational one. Naming it clearly is the first step toward addressing it deliberately.

examples.title: Emily Asks Which Clients Actually Choose Them for the Design
examples.scenario: 'We can offer clients everything under one roof.' Emily's potential partner described the design-build opportunity over the phone: her studio would handle design, his construction management firm would handle the build. A term sheet was on her desk. Before agreeing, she asked him a question: which of her clients in the past three years had chosen the studio specifically for the design, and which had asked about construction management? The answer was immediate and one-sided. Every client in her file had hired a separate construction manager. Not one had come to her for both. The two client types were different people who valued different things. Her studio's activity system was built entirely around the former.
examples.whatToDo: Map the activities the design-build partnership would require: scheduling systems, site supervision culture, construction contract management. Check each against the studio's current activity system. The overlap reveals whether the capability fit is real or assumed before any term sheet is signed.
examples.whyItMatters: A design-build partnership adds a capability system the studio does not currently have. Building it requires adding scheduling, supervision, and contract expertise while maintaining the design capability the existing clients are paying for. Activity system mismatch shows up as diluted quality in both directions.

examples.title: Ryan's Board Checks the Capability Before the Budget
examples.scenario: At 9:00, Ryan presents the oncology unit proposal to the board. Two slides: rising cancer diagnosis rates in the county, forty minutes of travel time to the nearest oncology center. The case for the unit is obvious. A board member who is also a retired oncologist raises her hand and asks: can you list the five activities the unit would need to perform consistently to deliver safe oncology care? Ryan lists them: specialized oncology nurses, a radiation therapy facility, oncology pharmacy capability, a radiologist with oncology certification, and patient volume high enough to sustain specialist salaries. She then asks him to check each one against the hospital's current capability. By the third check, the room understands the gap is not a funding question. It is a decade-long capability build.
examples.whatToDo: Before the capability funding request, list the five most critical activities the new unit would require at a consistent quality level. Check each one against the current activity system. The ones not present are not budget items; they are the activity system the strategy would need to build before the unit can open safely.
examples.whyItMatters: Community demand for a service is not the same as a capability to deliver it. The question for the hospital board is not whether cancer patients need care locally but whether the activity system required to provide that care safely can be built at this hospital's scale without compromising the existing capability.

examples.title: Antoine's Online Cohort Shows What Did Not Transfer
examples.scenario: Six months after launching the online pilot, Antoine reviewed the graduation and placement numbers. Completion rate for the online cohort: forty-four percent. For the in-person program: eighty-eight percent. Employer partnership calls for the online cohort: three. For the in-person program in the same period: eleven. He had assumed the curriculum would work across both formats. The placement data said something different. The in-person program's results were driven by cohort accountability, joint debugging sessions, and a pair-programming culture that formed through daily proximity. Online, those interactions were optional. Employer calls had dropped because hiring managers had noticed that online graduates arrived without the collaborative habits the in-person graduates had built. The activity system that produced placement outcomes did not transfer.
examples.whatToDo: Before launching the next online cohort, name the three activity-system elements responsible for the in-person placement rate. For each one, design a specific equivalent the online format can actually deliver. If none of those equivalents are feasible within the online model, the online cohort is a different product that requires a different capability system built from the start.
examples.whyItMatters: A program format that looks the same on a course outline requires a completely different activity system when the delivery medium changes. Completion and placement outcomes are the evidence that the capability system either translated or did not.

examples.title: Catarina's Warehouse Gets the Product to the Shelf. It Stops There.
examples.scenario: The warehouse smelled of cardboard and cold storage, optimized for movement: pallets in, pallets out, routes planned to minimize truck idle time. Before: Catarina signed the retail supply agreement after a meeting where the margin projection looked strong. Her team was exceptional at distribution logistics: route planning, supplier relationships, cold chain management, and inventory turnover. After: the first season's sell-through data arrived. The product had moved from warehouse to shelf. It had not moved from shelf to basket. The retail buyer called to discuss promotional strategy. Catarina's team had no one who knew how to design a retail promotion, negotiate endcap placement, or build the packaging story that drives a consumer to pick up an unfamiliar product. The activity systems were completely different.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next retail supply agreement, list the activities required to move product from shelf to basket: promotional planning, endcap negotiation, consumer packaging decisions, retail buyer relationship management. Check whether any of these currently exist in the organization. The ones that do not are not services to hire; they are an activity system to build.
examples.whyItMatters: Distribution logistics and retail brand management are two activity systems that share a supply chain but require completely different organizational capabilities. Entering retail distribution without the second system in place produces a shelf presence that does not convert.

examples.title: Pavel Imagines What the Partner Curator Would Need and Finds the Gap
examples.scenario: You are running the thought experiment with Pavel. The donor proposal is for three touring exhibitions over five years. He imagines the first show arriving at a partner museum: the partner curator sends installation requirements three weeks out. The crates travel with a specialist conservator. The lighting specs require an electrician familiar with museum climate standards. The installation schedule requires a site supervisor who can adapt to a different building's constraints on the fly. Pavel's curatorial staff is exceptional at scholarly interpretation and permanent collection research. None of them had been asked to coordinate a multi-city installation logistics system. He asks his deputy: how long would it take to build the operational capability the touring program requires without pulling the curatorial team away from the research work that makes this museum worth visiting? The answer makes the donor proposal look different.
examples.whatToDo: Before accepting the touring exhibition proposal, list the activities a traveling show requires that the permanent collection model does not: logistics coordination, partner museum relations, on-site installation management, specialized conservation transport. Calculate the resource cost of building those capabilities against the cost of diverting curatorial staff from the research function. Name the trade-off explicitly before accepting.
examples.whyItMatters: A traveling exhibition capability requires an activity system built around operational flexibility and logistics precision. A permanent collection capability requires an activity system built around scholarly depth and interpretive quality. Building both simultaneously pulls the activity systems in opposite directions.

examples.title: Ingrid Reviews Two Years of Capability Mismatch
examples.scenario: Two years after launching the racing program, Ingrid reviewed the membership data. The coaching hire had left after fourteen months: the club's slip assignments prioritized recreational members by seniority, which created regular availability conflicts for the racing fleet. Of the twenty-four competitive members who joined in the first year, eighteen had departed. Their resignation notes cited the same two issues: coaching inconsistency and facility conflicts. The recreational membership had grown. The racing program had collapsed. The capability fit problem had been visible before the launch if anyone had listed the five activities a competitive racing program required and checked them against the club's facility configuration, slip allocation system, and coaching hire model.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next program expansion, list the five activity-system requirements the new program cannot run without: dedicated slip allocation, coaching credentials and schedule continuity, racing-specific equipment maintenance, a competition calendar that does not conflict with recreational booking. Check each against what the club currently has. The ones missing are conditions that must exist before the program is viable, not items to address after the launch.
examples.whyItMatters: A recreational sailing club and a competitive racing program are two activity systems housed in the same facility. Adding the second without building the activity system it requires produces a program that the facility's existing configuration will reliably undermine.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a strategy-specific capability system from a general list of organizational strengths?
choices: A capability system includes only capabilities the organization is currently investing to build; a strength list includes historical capabilities.
A capability system is defined by working backward from the how-to-win choice to identify specific required activities; a strength list is assembled from what the organization currently does well.
A capability system is a ranked list of the organization's top strengths sorted by relevance to current market conditions.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is the direction of the analysis. A strength list starts from what exists. A capability system starts from what the strategy requires and works backward. Strengths that do not connect to the how-to-win choice are costs, not advantages, regardless of how well-developed they are.

questions.prompt: When a software company's how-to-win choice is to be the most reliable platform for financial services teams, what backward-design question identifies the capabilities that must be in place?
choices: What must the company be able to do consistently well for financial services teams to choose this platform over alternatives when downtime risk is their primary concern?

What features do our financial services customers most frequently request in product reviews, since aggregated user feedback is the most direct signal about which capability gaps are limiting renewals in the target segment?

What is the company's current best technical capability that already differentiates it in the enterprise market, since building outward from existing strength is more efficient than trying to develop capabilities from scratch under a new strategy?
questions.explanation: The backward-mapping question starts from the how-to-win choice (reliability for downtime-averse financial teams) and asks what activity system must exist to deliver that specific advantage. Feature requests and current differentiators are both useful but describe what exists, not what the strategy requires for this specific field and customer.

questions.prompt: The coding bootcamp's in-person program achieves eighty-eight percent completion. The new online cohort is at fifty-two percent completion. What is the strategic diagnosis?
choices: Online learners are inherently less motivated than in-person learners and require stronger incentive structures, so the cohort needs sharper completion incentives and milestone tracking to lift completion to the in-person rate.

The online cohort needs a better candidate screening process to attract more committed applicants, since the gap is largely a candidate-quality issue and tighter admissions would produce completion numbers closer to the in-person results.
The in-person activity system (cohort accountability, pair programming, proximity-built habits) did not transfer; the online format needs a different activity system built for it.
questions.explanation: Motivation and screening are not the root cause. The completion and placement data reveal an activity system problem: the in-person program's results depend on activities that the online format cannot replicate without being redesigned. The online cohort needs its own capability system built for its specific format, not a copy of the in-person one.

questions.prompt: The specialty food distributor signs a retail supply agreement. After the first season, sell-through is forty percent below projection. What is the strategic diagnosis?
choices: The distributor's activity system was built for logistics, not the consumer brand decisions that move product from shelf to basket; the two systems were never audited against each other before the agreement was signed.

The distributor needs to hire a retail marketing consultant to provide promotional expertise for the current season, because the immediate gap is in-store execution and an experienced consultant can stand up the missing capability before the season ends.

The distributor moved too quickly; a consumer brand division should have been built before approaching retailers, since the activity-system gap was visible upfront and a staged build would have closed it before the shelf commitment.
questions.explanation: A staffing gap or timing error are operational diagnoses. The case reveals an activity system mismatch: distribution logistics and retail brand management require fundamentally different activities. Signing the retail agreement without auditing the capability gap produced a predictable result: a shelf presence the missing consumer brand system could not convert to a purchase.

questions.prompt: P&G's acquisition of Gillette was justified on the basis of capability fit. Which question best represents the backward-mapping logic that made the acquisition compelling?
choices: Is Gillette the largest available acquisition target in a category adjacent to P&G's existing portfolio, since scale is the dominant factor in shaving-category economics and the acquisition that produces the most absolute volume is the most strategically valuable?
Do Gillette's specific capabilities (precision manufacturing, consumer insight, global distribution) reinforce the activities P&G's how-to-win choices require in their target consumer categories?

Will acquiring Gillette produce the highest revenue synergies available in the current acquisition environment, because synergy math is the language investors use to evaluate large deals and the deal with the highest projected number will produce the strongest endorsement?
questions.explanation: Acquisition size and revenue synergies are financial metrics, not strategic ones. The backward-mapping logic asks whether Gillette's activity system reinforces P&G's required capabilities. Gillette fit because the things Gillette could do well were specifically the things P&G's strategy needed done, not because of market position or brand value alone.

questions.prompt: The rural hospital's administrator lists five activities an oncology unit would require: oncology-trained nursing, chemotherapy preparation pharmacy, radiation coordination, patient navigation, and clinical research connection. The hospital has only the first two. What does this audit imply?
choices: The community demand justifies building the three missing capabilities before the unit opens, since unmet demand is a strong signal that investment will produce returns and the hospital can phase the capability build over the first year of operation.

The hospital should partner with a regional cancer center to fill the gaps temporarily, because a partnership produces immediate capability coverage while the hospital decides whether to develop the activity system permanently on its own.
The audit reveals an activity system the hospital does not have; building it is a strategic decision (not a budget item) that must be made before the unit is approved.
questions.explanation: Community demand does not resolve a capability gap. Temporary partnerships are operational tools, not strategic answers. The backward-mapping audit revealed that the oncology unit requires an activity system the hospital does not have. Building it is a decade-long commitment that must be evaluated as a strategic choice, not as a service addition.

questions.prompt: When an architecture studio is considering a design-build partnership that requires the studio to manage construction logistics, scheduling, and contractor relationships, what is the right strategic move?
choices: List the activities construction management requires (scheduling systems, site supervision, contract management) and check each against the studio's current activity system to identify the gap before deciding.

Survey current clients about whether they would prefer a single vendor for design and construction services, since direct client demand is the strongest signal that the integrated offering will earn enough revenue to justify the capability build.

Ask the construction management partner to handle all construction activities so the studio only needs to contribute design, since a clean division of responsibility lets the studio capture the integrated-offering revenue without building any new capability internally.
questions.explanation: Client surveys identify demand, not capability fit. Delegating to the partner avoids the audit entirely. The capability audit must list the activities the partnership requires from the studio's side and check whether those activities exist in the current system. That check determines whether the partnership adds a genuine capability or exposes a gap.

questions.prompt: The sailing club adds a competitive racing program. After two years, the coach reports that ranked finishes are below the regional average. The club has recreational members who hold most slip leases. What is the strategic diagnosis?
choices: The club hired the wrong coach and needs to improve its recruiting process for the next hire, since coaching quality is the most visible determinant of competitive results and a stronger hire would lift performance without changing the club's structure.
The racing program needed dedicated slips, coaching continuity, and fleet priority: an activity system the recreational club's setup could not support; no capability audit was done before launch.

The recreational membership's seniority-based slip allocation is unfair to competitive members and should be restructured, since the existing allocation rule blocks the racing program from getting the resources it needs to develop competitive results.
questions.explanation: A hiring error or a policy change are operational diagnoses. The strategic diagnosis is an activity system mismatch: the racing program required a facility configuration and resource allocation that the recreational club's existing system could not accommodate without being restructured. The capability audit should have identified this before the program launched.

questions.prompt: The museum director is evaluating a donor proposal for three touring exhibitions over five years. The current activity system is built around a permanent collection. What is the right strategic move?
choices: Accept the proposal because donor relationships are strategically important and capability gaps can be addressed as they arise, since the donor's continued support is contingent on visible engagement and the museum's standing in the donor community depends on willingness to take on ambitious projects.

Accept one touring exhibition as a pilot and evaluate whether the capability can be built from the experience, since a single project produces real learning about the activity-system gap without committing the museum to the full three-exhibition obligation upfront.

Map the activities a touring show requires against the current system, name the gaps, and decide whether building the touring capability reinforces or dilutes the permanent collection strategy before accepting.
questions.explanation: Accepting for donor relationship reasons or piloting without the capability audit both skip the strategic question. The evaluation must start from the backward-mapping question: what does the touring capability require, and does building it reinforce or draw from the activity system the permanent collection strategy depends on? That answer determines whether the proposal is a strategic fit or a capability distraction.

reviewCards.front: What is a strategy-specific capability system?
reviewCards.back: The specific set of activities the organization must perform at a consistently high level for its how-to-win choice to deliver a genuine advantage. It is defined by working backward from the strategy, not assembled from what the organization currently does well.

reviewCards.front: What backward-mapping question identifies required capabilities?
reviewCards.back: What must the organization be able to do well, specifically and consistently, for the how-to-win choice to work in the chosen field? The answer defines the required capability system and reveals where the gaps are.

reviewCards.front: What made the Gillette acquisition a strategic capability fit for P&G?
reviewCards.back: Gillette's activity system reinforced what P&G's strategy needed done. The fit was in specific capabilities (precision manufacturing, consumer insight, global distribution) that pointed in the same direction as P&G's how-to-win choices, not in Gillette's brand size or market position alone.

reviewCards.front: Name two effects of adding a new offering without auditing the activity system first.
reviewCards.back: The new offering requires capabilities the organization does not have. The gap shows up as diluted performance in the new offering and as resources drawn away from the activity system the existing strategy depends on. Both suffer.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between a strength and a required capability?
reviewCards.back: A strength is something the organization does well. A required capability is something the strategy needs done well to produce advantage in the chosen field. A strength that does not connect to the how-to-win choice creates cost, not advantage.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to audit capabilities by working backward from the how-to-win choice, not forward from a list of current strengths. You practice the backward-mapping question and apply it to identify specific capability gaps before committing to a new offering, partnership, or expansion.

ifThenPlans.context: evaluating a new service or product offering
ifThenPlans.plan: Before committing, list the activities the new offering would require from the organization at a consistently high level. Check each one against the existing activity system. The ones not present are not items to add later; they are capabilities that must be built before the offering can be delivered at the quality the strategy requires.

ifThenPlans.context: reviewing a proposed acquisition or partnership
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask whether the acquisition or partner's specific capabilities reinforce the activities your how-to-win choice requires. If the activities point in the same direction, the fit is real. If the acquired capabilities require a different activity system, the acquisition is a distraction from the existing strategy.

ifThenPlans.context: allocating development budget across multiple capabilities
ifThenPlans.plan: Start from the how-to-win choice and list the capabilities it requires. Allocate the development budget to those first. Investment in a capability that is not required by the strategy is overhead regardless of how well-developed it is.

ifThenPlans.context: deciding whether to pursue a new customer segment or channel
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask whether serving the new segment requires the same activity system as the current strategy or a different one. A different activity system means a second strategy that must be evaluated on its own terms, not an extension of the first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: State your current how-to-win choice in one sentence. Then name the three specific activities your organization must perform at a high level for that choice to work. For each one, rate honestly: have it, building it, or not yet started. The ones not yet started are the gaps the investment conversation should be about.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: When a new opportunity, request, or partnership comes up, run the backward-mapping question before deciding. Ask what activities the new opportunity requires from your organization and whether those activities reinforce or pull from the current capability system. Name the answer before saying yes.

memorableLines.text: Leon was not weak in the other three areas. He was diluting the one area that made the firm irreplaceable.
Gillette fit because the things Gillette was able to do well were the specific things P&G's strategy needed done.
An isolated strength that does not connect to the how-to-win choice creates cost, not advantage.

chapters.title: Manage What Matters
chapters.hook: Green dashboard: revenue up, NPS steady. Three of four strategic choices reversed by daily decisions. No metric for that.
chapters.counterintuition: A management system that everyone follows exactly can still kill a strategy. When the reviews, measures, and rewards were built for the previous strategic choices, every team member doing their job correctly is compounding the problem.
chapters.tryThisNow: After your next review meeting, list the three things that were measured or reported. Ask: if the strategy were actually working, which of those numbers would look different? If none would change, the system is reporting on the past, not reinforcing the strategy. Name one decision the review should have forced and did not.
chapters.keyTakeaway: The management system is the fifth strategic choice: the reviews, measures, and rewards that must reinforce the first four, or they will quietly undo them.

breakdown.fastRead:
Simon's retail chain had changed its strategy eighteen months ago: from new customer acquisition to loyalty and repeat purchase depth. The choices were approved by the board. The commission structure was not updated. The team was still paid for new accounts.

Every quarterly review showed green: acquisition targets hit, new accounts up, team morale positive. The loyalty metrics were not on any review slide.

Eighteen months after the strategy changed, the top three performers by commission were the three reps who had done the least work on repeat customer engagement.

A strategy is not complete when the choices are made. It is complete when the management systems reward the behavior the choices require.
breakdown.deepRead:
The fifth strategic choice is the management system: the reviews, measures, and accountability routines that reinforce the first four choices or quietly undermine them. A management system becomes a problem not by failing but by succeeding at the wrong thing. If the reviews measure the previous strategy's priorities and the compensation rewards the previous strategy's behaviors, the system performs exactly as designed: driving effort toward the old direction while the new strategy is officially in place.

The distinction between a genuine strategy review and corporate theater is whether the review could actually change a decision. A review that cannot change a decision is not a strategy review. It is a briefing.

The difference shows up in the questions being asked. A genuine strategy review asks: is this working and why? It invites new information that might reverse a decision. Corporate theater asks: are we on track to the plan we already committed to? That question defends a position and validates work already done. The review may surface a problem. But the format has no mechanism for using that problem to change what the organization does next.

A review built for the previous strategy performs corporate theater regardless of the new strategic language used to describe it. The measures were designed to report on different choices. The accountability routines ask questions the previous strategy needed answered. The decisions most in need of revisiting are the ones the review format cannot raise.
breakdown.fullRead:
Management systems are the most common way a strategy is killed without anyone deciding to kill it. The strategic choices are made. The leadership team approves them. Execution begins. And then the reviews continue to measure the previous strategy's metrics, the compensation continues to reward the previous strategy's behavior, and the accountability routines continue to ask the questions the previous strategy needed answered.

No one decides to undermine the new strategy. The system does it automatically, because the system was never updated to point in the new direction.

The test for any management system is one question: if the strategy were actually working, which of these numbers would look different? If the answer is none of the numbers the system currently tracks, the system is not reinforcing the strategy. It is a legacy measurement running undisturbed while the strategy tries to move in a different direction.

A sales organization that shifts from new account acquisition to renewal and expansion revenue but keeps its commission structure weighted toward new accounts will have a clear outcome: the team will optimize for new accounts. The measure drives the behavior. If the behavior the measure drives is not the behavior the strategy requires, the system is working perfectly in the wrong direction.

Think about the last review meeting you participated in. What were the three main things reported? Were they things that would look different if the new strategy were working, or things that measured adherence to a plan already committed to? If the answer is adherence, the review was not checking whether the strategy is working. It was confirming that everyone did what they agreed to do. Those are different conversations. Only the first one can change what happens next.

The second test is whether the review could have reversed a decision. If every agenda item was a confirmation of a committed plan, the meeting was a briefing. If at least one agenda item allowed the group to look at evidence and ask whether the strategic choice is working, the meeting was a strategy review. The difference is not the frequency or the attendees. It is whether new information could change a decision that was previously made.

Reviews that cannot change decisions are not neutral. They actively reinforce whatever direction the current metrics point. If those metrics were designed for the previous strategy, the review is reinforcing the previous strategy every time it runs, at every level of the organization, without anyone intending it to.

Name one review that your team runs regularly. Ask what decision it could change if the information were worse than expected. If the answer is nothing changes, the review is corporate theater. That is not a judgment; it is a design problem. The management system can be redesigned to ask the question the strategy requires.

examples.title: Rachel Sees Six Months of Green Velocity and Declining Retention
examples.scenario: Rachel reviewed six months of sprint decks. Every single one celebrated a green velocity number in the top right corner. Every single one was missing the retention chart. She went back to the retention data separately and found that the rate had declined in four of the six months covered by those green reviews. The team had been accountable for throughput and hitting targets on throughput. No one had been accountable for retention depth because retention depth was not on any review slide. The system had reinforced exactly the wrong behavior: building faster toward the old strategic priority while the new one slowly worsened.
examples.whatToDo: Replace velocity as the primary sprint review metric with the retention depth measure the new strategy requires. Remove throughput reporting from the standard review agenda or move it to an appendix. The change signals to the team which behavior the review now holds them accountable for.
examples.whyItMatters: A review format that measures the previous strategy's priorities rewards the previous strategy's behavior regardless of what strategic choices were made six months ago. The sprint review is not a neutral report; it is the system that tells the team what they are accountable for.

examples.title: Luke Asks Which Number Would Change If the New Strategy Were Working
examples.scenario: At 2:00 p.m., Luke walks into the monthly leadership review and sees the standard agenda printed on the table: bed occupancy, procedure counts, average length of stay. Three numbers. All three were designed to measure acute treatment volume. He sits down and asks the group a question before the first slide: which of those three numbers would look different next month if our preventive care initiative were working? Silence. Then someone says: none of them. The systems are reporting on the old strategy. The new one is invisible, unmeasured, and unaccountable.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next monthly review, name the one or two measures that would show the preventive care initiative is gaining traction: early-intervention referral counts, screening completion rates, patient re-enrollment in wellness programs. Replace one of the existing agenda items with one of those measures to make the new strategy visible in the review.
examples.whyItMatters: A review that cannot show whether the new strategy is working is not a strategy review. It is a performance report for the previous strategy. The gap becomes visible when the question is asked: which of these numbers would look different if the new strategy were working?

examples.title: Niklas Hears What the Commission Structure Is Actually Saying
examples.scenario: 'I spend seventy percent of my time on renewal calls. I get paid for zero percent of it.' Niklas's top rep said it quietly after the team meeting, not in front of the room. She was not complaining about the work. She was pointing at the management system. The commission report from last quarter showed her at the bottom: the lowest new-deal commission of anyone on the team. The renewal-rate leaderboard showed her at the top. The new strategy said renewal and expansion were the priority. The commission structure said new accounts were. She was about to start job-searching because the system was telling her the new strategy was not the real one.
examples.whatToDo: Redesign the commission structure so renewal and expansion revenue carries equal or greater weight than new account acquisition. The change does not require announcing a new culture; it requires changing the number that appears on the rep's commission statement. That is the communication that changes behavior.
examples.whyItMatters: A commission structure is not a neutral financial instrument. It is the management system's most direct communication about which behavior the strategy actually values. When the commission and the stated strategy point in different directions, the commission wins.

examples.title: Paula Rebuilds the Client Review to Show What the New Position Requires
examples.scenario: The conference room smells of cold coffee and printed slide decks: nine slides of deliverable checkboxes and one slide that says campaign results: data collection ongoing. Before: Paula runs the client review showing on-time delivery rates and budget variance. Both are green. The client asks for the third time whether the campaign moved any customer behavior.
