The review format has no answer for that question. It was designed for an agency that sold outputs. The new positioning sells effectiveness. After: Paula rebuilds the review template around two leading effectiveness indicators she can report monthly: behavioral signal rate from the campaign's target cohort and assisted conversion attribution. The client stops asking the question because the review now answers it.
examples.whatToDo: Identify the one or two leading indicators of effectiveness that the new strategic position requires the agency to report. Replace the delivery compliance slides with those indicators in the standard client review template. The new format is the management system that makes the new position visible and accountable.
examples.whyItMatters: A client review built around delivery compliance reinforces a delivery-focused strategic position even when the agency has formally committed to an effectiveness-focused one. The review format is not cosmetic; it is the system that determines what the agency is accountable for in every client relationship.

examples.title: Janek's Promotion Data Shows Three Years of the Wrong Strategy
examples.scenario: Janek reviewed three years of promotion committee notes. Every faculty member promoted to associate professor had a strong publications record and weak industry involvement. Two faculty members with strong industry partnership records and moderate publication counts had been denied in the same period. The committee had made reasonable decisions given the criteria the system used. But the criteria were the criteria of the research-ranking strategy the department had formally changed two years ago. The promotion system had made the decision every year that the management system required: reward publications. The new strategy was on the letterhead. It was not in the rubric.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next promotion cycle, revise the review rubric to include industry partnership outcomes at a weight that reflects the new strategic emphasis. The change must be in the rubric, not in the committee's instructions. Instructions are interpreted; rubrics are applied.
examples.whyItMatters: A promotion system that measures citation counts and journal tier for a department that has committed to an industry partnership strategy will systematically produce promotion decisions that reward the old strategy. The pattern shows up across multiple cycles, not as individual errors but as a management system performing exactly as designed.

examples.title: Camille Imagines the Combined P&L Conversation and Sees the Problem
examples.scenario: You imagine standing at the whiteboard in front of Camille's father, the founder, presenting the combined month-end P&L. The new product line has low margins and fast growth. The mature line has high margins and slow growth. Combined, they produce a number that looks mediocre. Camille has run this mental exercise three times. Each time she gets to the margin line, she can predict the conversation: the new line's losses will trigger a cost-cutting discussion that will pull investment from exactly the initiative that needs it most. The management system does not distinguish two different strategies. It treats both product lines as one. Every month the combined P&L sends the same signal: the margins are lower than they should be. Every month the new line loses the investment argument.
examples.whatToDo: Separate the two product lines in the monthly review structure and use different performance measures for each based on their respective strategic positions. Present the mature line on margin and cash contribution. Present the new line on revenue growth rate and market signal indicators. The review must distinguish two strategies to reinforce both.
examples.whyItMatters: A combined P&L that aggregates two lines with different strategic profiles makes the new line look like a problem every time its low margins are averaged against the mature line's high ones. The review structure is suppressing investment in the growth strategy by measuring it against the wrong standard.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a genuine strategy review from corporate theater?
choices: A genuine strategy review could actually change a decision based on new information; corporate theater validates adherence to an already-committed plan and cannot generate new decisions.

A genuine strategy review focuses on long-term metrics; corporate theater focuses on short-term quarterly performance, since short-term metrics encourage tactical reactions while long-term metrics force the organization to defend its strategic position.

A genuine strategy review is led by the CEO; corporate theater is delegated to middle management reporting, because leader presence signals that strategic decisions are actually on the table while delegated reviews become status updates without authority to change direction.
questions.explanation: The defining characteristic is whether new information in the review can change what the organization decides to do. A review designed to validate adherence to a plan asks whether we are on track, not whether the track is right. That question defends a committed position and cannot generate new decisions, which is the definition of corporate theater.

questions.prompt: When a sales organization shifted strategy from new account acquisition to renewal and expansion six months ago, but renewal rates have not improved, what is the strategic move?
choices: Brief the team on the new strategy at the next all-hands and reinforce the importance of renewal focus, since clear communication of the strategic shift is the first lever and most reps will adjust behavior once they understand what leadership is asking for.
Redesign the commission structure so that renewal and expansion revenue carries equal or greater weight than new account acquisition, aligning the reward with the new strategic choice.

Add renewal rates to the monthly performance dashboard alongside new account metrics and report both, because visibility on the new metric is the first step and reps will adjust effort once renewal performance becomes part of the conversation.
questions.explanation: Briefing the team changes awareness, not incentive. Adding renewals to the dashboard without changing the commission leaves the existing reward in place. The management system must change the compensation, not just the reporting, to make the new strategic behavior the one that gets rewarded.

questions.prompt: The product team shifted strategy from feature velocity to retention depth six months ago. The sprint review still leads with velocity metrics. What is the strategic move?
choices: Continue the current sprint review format but add a verbal retention update at the end of each meeting, since verbal reinforcement of the new priority is enough to shift attention without disrupting the team's established sprint rhythm.

Replace the sprint review with a monthly strategic review covering all product metrics at once, because a less frequent and broader review forces the team to think strategically rather than tactically and surfaces retention conversations naturally alongside other metrics.
Replace velocity as the primary sprint review metric with the retention depth measure the new strategy requires, and remove throughput reporting from the standard agenda.
questions.explanation: A verbal update leaves velocity as the primary metric, which still signals what the team is accountable for. A monthly strategic review does not change the sprint review that is reinforcing the old strategy every two weeks. Replacing the primary metric removes the old reward signal and puts the new strategy's required measure at the center of the review.

questions.prompt: The hospital department shifted strategic emphasis from acute treatment volume to preventive care integration twelve months ago. The monthly leadership review still emphasizes acute-care throughput. What is the strategic problem?
choices: The review measures what mattered under the old strategy, making the leadership team accountable for the old strategy's outputs while the new one remains invisible and unreinforced in the management system.

The leadership team lacks commitment to the preventive care initiative and needs stronger direction from the chief medical officer, since the new strategy requires top-down advocacy to move attention away from acute-care metrics that the team has worked with for years.

The preventive care initiative needs more time to generate measurable outcomes before it can be incorporated into the leadership review, since meaningful preventive-care results take eighteen to twenty-four months to appear and reviewing them earlier would be premature.
questions.explanation: Commitment and timeline are not the primary diagnosis. The review measures the old strategy's priorities and holds leaders accountable for the old strategy's outputs. The new strategy has no measure in the review, which means it has no reinforcement mechanism. The management system is actively rewarding the old direction, not failing to reward the new one.

questions.prompt: When a creative agency shifted from output quantity to campaign effectiveness, but the client review still emphasizes deliverables, what is the strategic move?
choices: Add a slide at the end of the client review showing effectiveness metrics collected so far, since visibility on effectiveness alongside deliverables creates a baseline the agency can build on as the new strategy matures.
Replace deliverable completion and budget adherence with effectiveness measures the agency can report monthly, making the review accountable to the new strategic position.

Schedule a separate effectiveness review alongside the existing delivery review to address the client's recurring question, because a parallel review surfaces the strategic conversation without disrupting the operational accountability the existing review provides.
questions.explanation: A slide at the end or a parallel review both leave the primary template in place, continuing to reward delivery compliance. The management system change must make effectiveness the primary measure in the client review and remove the delivery measures that reinforce the old strategic position. Adding alongside is not alignment; it is addition.

questions.prompt: The university department formally committed to industry partnership outcomes alongside research output two years ago. Three promotion cycles later, the faculty member with the strongest partnership record was passed over. What is the strategic diagnosis?
choices: The promotion system weighted publications and ignored partnership outcomes: three years of decisions rewarding the old research-first strategy while leadership formally committed to a different one.

The promotion committee made reasonable decisions given the evidence available at each review cycle, since publication records are the most measurable form of academic productivity and the committee correctly weighted the evidence in front of it.

The department needs to clarify the new strategic emphasis to the promotion committee before the next cycle, since the committee is following the criteria it was given and updated communication of the new priorities will adjust the next round of decisions.
questions.explanation: The committee decisions were correct given the criteria the system used. The problem is the criteria themselves: promotion processes built for the old strategy reward the old behavior regardless of what leadership formally commits to. Three years of data show a systematic management system problem, not a series of individual committee errors.

questions.prompt: The family business presents both a mature product line and a new product line in the same monthly P&L review. The new line is consistently underweighted in conversation. What is the strategic move?
choices: Adjust the new product line's margin targets to be closer to the mature line's historical margins, since aligned margin expectations would let the review compare both lines on the same scale and produce a clearer performance picture.

Continue combined reporting for one more year before evaluating whether separation is warranted, since the new product line is too early in its trajectory to be evaluated independently and the combined view smooths volatility during the ramp.
Separate the two product lines in the review, apply metrics suited to each line's strategic profile, and present them independently so each is evaluated on its own terms.
questions.explanation: Adjusting margin targets holds the new line to the wrong standard. Waiting extends the period in which combined reporting suppresses investment in the growth line. The management system must separate the lines so the different strategies governing each can be measured and rewarded independently, without one line's performance penalizing the other.

questions.prompt: The sales director's top-performing rep by commission has the lowest renewal rate. The renewal-focused rep earns thirty percent less. What is the strategic diagnosis?
choices: The top-performing rep has a more effective approach and the organization should recognize and replicate that pattern, since high commission earnings are evidence of customer demand and the rep's approach is generating revenue the organization needs.

The commission structure is actively rewarding the behavior the new strategy wants to eliminate and penalizing the behavior the new strategy requires, making the management system work directly against the strategic choice.

The renewal-focused rep needs additional coaching to improve new account performance alongside renewal work, since strong reps deliver on both dimensions and the gap in new-account numbers is a development opportunity for the renewal-focused rep.
questions.explanation: The commission-to-renewal inversion reveals that the management system rewards the old strategic behavior and penalizes the new one. This is not a rep capability problem; it is a design problem. The system is performing exactly as designed: rewarding new account acquisition, which is the opposite of what the new strategy requires.

questions.prompt: The hospital department chief has two options: Option A, add early-intervention metrics to the existing acute-care review alongside acute-care throughput; Option B, replace acute-care throughput with early-intervention metrics as the primary review topic. Which is the stronger strategic option, and why?
choices: Option A, because it shows the leadership team is taking the new strategy seriously without disrupting the accountability structure that already works, since gradual change reduces the risk of operational disruption during a strategic transition.

Both equally, because each addresses the management system gap in a way appropriate to different organizational contexts, and the right answer depends on the department's tolerance for disruption to existing accountability routines.

Option B, because Option A adds preventive care measures without removing the acute care metrics that still drive the primary accountability signal; the old strategy's rewards remain fully intact and the review continues to primarily reinforce the previous direction.
questions.explanation: Option A adds new measurement without removing the old measure. The existing metrics still dominate the review's accountability logic, meaning the old strategy's rewards remain active. Option B redesigns the review to reinforce the new strategy and removes the mechanism that continues to reward the old one. Management system alignment requires replacing the old rewards, not adding new ones alongside them.

reviewCards.front: What distinguishes a strategy review from corporate theater?
reviewCards.back: A strategy review is one that could actually change a decision based on new information. Corporate theater validates adherence to a plan already committed to. The difference shows up in the question being asked: is this working and why, or are we on track to what we already agreed?

reviewCards.front: What is the management system test for strategy alignment?
reviewCards.back: Ask: if the strategy were actually working, which of the numbers the system currently tracks would look different? If none would change, the system is measuring the previous strategy's priorities, not reinforcing the new one.

reviewCards.front: What happens when a commission structure is not updated after a strategic shift?
reviewCards.back: The commission continues to reward the old strategy's behavior. The team optimizes for what the commission pays for. The new strategy's priorities are reported but not rewarded, which means they are not fully pursued regardless of what the leadership team communicates.

reviewCards.front: Name three management system elements that most often undermine a new strategy passively.
reviewCards.back: Reviews measure what the previous strategy needed tracked. Compensation rewards what the previous strategy valued. Accountability routines ask questions the previous strategy needed answered. The system rewards the old direction automatically, with no one deciding to undermine the new one.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean when a review could not force any decision?
reviewCards.back: It means the review was a briefing, not a strategy review. A review that cannot change what the organization decides to do next is a performance report for the previous strategy, not a management system aligned to the new one.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to audit management systems by asking which behavior each review, measure, and accountability routine currently rewards and whether that behavior is the behavior the strategy requires. You practice the alignment test: if the strategy were actually working, which numbers would look different?

ifThenPlans.context: after a strategic choice is made or approved
ifThenPlans.plan: Before ending the planning session, name the one review, measure, or accountability routine that most needs to change for the new strategy to be reinforced. Schedule that change in the same planning cycle, not as a later implementation task.

ifThenPlans.context: when a team is consistently not executing a new strategic direction
ifThenPlans.plan: Check whether the compensation, review structure, or accountability system is still rewarding the old behavior. Consistent non-execution is more often a management system problem than a commitment problem.

ifThenPlans.context: when designing a new performance review format
ifThenPlans.plan: Start with the strategic choices, not with the available metrics. Ask which specific behaviors the strategy requires and design the review to make those behaviors visible and accountable. Remove metrics that reinforce different strategic priorities.

ifThenPlans.context: when a review shows green across all metrics but strategic progress is unclear
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask which green metric would look different if the new strategy were actually working. If none would change, the review is measuring the wrong things and the strategy is invisible to the management system.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: After your next team review, write down the three things the review measured or reported. For each one, ask: would this number look different if the strategy were working? If none would change, name one specific measure that would show strategic progress and one specific review question that could not be answered today.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, after a review meeting or performance check-in, ask whether the questions being asked could have changed a decision. If the questions were all about adherence to an already-committed plan, the review was corporate theater. Name one question the review should have asked but did not.

memorableLines.text: A strategy is not complete when the choices are made. It is complete when the management systems reward the behavior the choices require.
A review that cannot change a decision is not a strategy review. It is a briefing.
The test for any management system is one question: if the strategy were actually working, which of these numbers would look different?

chapters.title: Think Through Strategy
chapters.hook: The board presentation was ninety slides long. Forty-two of those slides were analysis of the preferred option. There was no second option, so there was nothing to analyze.
chapters.counterintuition: The common assumption is that more rigorous analysis produces better strategy. The problem is that analysis and possibility-generation are different activities. Analysis tells you whether a possibility holds up. It cannot tell you what possibilities exist. When analysis runs before possibilities are generated, it does not produce a strategy; it produces a rationalization: a set of arguments for the option the team had already mentally selected. The result looks thorough and is not strategic.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before your next strategic decision, write down three genuinely different options: not the main option and two alternatives that are clearly weaker. If you cannot name three options that each have a real argument in their favor, you have not yet done strategic thinking. Start with the one option you almost never consider.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Strategic thinking requires generating at least two or three genuinely different possibilities before analyzing any of them; analysis that runs before possibilities exist does not produce strategy, it produces rationalization of the option already in the room.

breakdown.fastRead:
Vera ran a graphic design studio and had spent three weeks analyzing whether to stay focused on brand identity work: the revenue model, the pipeline, the competitive landscape. The analysis told her the brand identity path was defensible. What it could not tell her was whether a packaging-design focus or a motion-graphics specialization would win a different and larger part of the market. Vera had spent three weeks analyzing whether the brand identity path was viable. She had not yet spent three hours imagining what the packaging path would look like as a real strategy. That is not a gap in analysis. That is the absence of strategic thinking.

The core move is simple to state and difficult to do: generate at least two or three genuinely different strategic options before analyzing any of them. The examples above show what happens when that step is skipped. Anna had twelve studies and one route. Sam had a brand equity report and one option. Isabel had four months of committee work on one curriculum philosophy. In each case, the analysis was real and the strategic thinking had not started yet.
breakdown.deepRead:
The misunderstanding worth correcting is the belief that rigorous analysis produces strategy. Analysis and possibility-generation are distinct activities that happen in a specific sequence: possibilities first, analysis second. When analysis runs before possibilities are generated, it becomes rationalization: a structured argument for the option that was already in the room.

The five questions of the strategy cascade (winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, capabilities, management systems) do not form a checklist where the first question is answered and the next one begins. They form a logic flow that runs in both directions. Answering the where-to-play question may require reopening the winning aspiration. Settling on a how-to-win choice may reveal that the initial where-to-play was too narrow. This is why generating multiple genuine possibilities, each a complete cascade across all five questions, is more useful than perfecting a single option. The five questions do not run in one direction. Answering where to play may reopen what winning looks like. That is not a flaw in the logic. That is what the logic is for.

The analysis comes second.

The practical test is whether the options on the table have distinct strategic logic. Two options that target the same customer with the same how-to-win logic and differ only in price are not two genuine possibilities. They are one default with a footnote. Genuine alternatives have different where-to-play choices, different how-to-win logic, or both.
breakdown.fullRead:
The insight that analysis cannot generate possibilities is easier to accept than to apply. In practice, most strategy processes begin with an option that arrived through some combination of prior commitment, organizational momentum, and convenience. The process that follows is then designed to evaluate that option. This is not dishonest. It is how organizations work. The problem is that a process designed to evaluate one option cannot produce a better option. It can only confirm or abandon what it started with. The strategic question, which is which option to pursue, never gets asked because only one option is present.

The six examples above share a structural feature. In each case, the person responsible for the strategic decision had access to analysis that was real, well-constructed, and useful. And in each case, they lacked the thing that analysis cannot produce: a second genuine option to evaluate. Anna's twelve studies were thorough and answered questions only about the preferred route. Sam's brand equity report was accurate and informed only the decision about the current brand. Isabel's committee work was responsible and evaluated only the curriculum philosophy that had been chosen before the committee met. None of it amounted to strategic thinking, because strategic thinking requires a choice between genuine possibilities, not an evaluation of one.

Here is what genuine possibilities require. Each option needs a coherent answer to the winning aspiration question: which specific customers, and what specific outcome for them. Each option needs a where-to-play answer that is genuinely different from the other options, not a minor variation on the same field. Each option needs a how-to-win logic that explains why a customer would choose this option over the alternative. And each option needs, at minimum, a rough sketch of the capabilities required to execute it. A sentence explaining why an alternative was not pursued due to scale limitations is not a genuine possibility. It is a closed door with no room described behind it.

The iterative nature of the strategy logic flow matters here. The five strategic questions are not answered in sequence and locked. Answering the where-to-play question may require reopening the winning aspiration. A how-to-win choice may reveal that the initial where-to-play was too narrow. This is why each genuine option should be sketched as a complete cascade, not as a one-sentence alternative. An option that names only a different customer segment is not a strategic possibility. An option that names which segment, why they would choose you, what capabilities are required, and what winning looks like for that segment is a genuine possibility worth analyzing.

Consider the decision you are currently working toward. How many options are actually on the table? Not how many were mentioned in a meeting, not how many appear in an appendix, but how many have been worked out to the level of having a real argument in their favor. If the answer is one, the strategic thinking has not started. The work before analysis is generating at least two options that a reasonable person could choose and defend. The question is not whether your preferred option holds up under analysis. The question is whether the other options were real enough to lose to it.

The hardest part of this prescription is generating the option you almost never consider. The default option arrives with a constituency, with prior work behind it, with organizational memory supporting it. The genuine alternative has to be built from scratch, usually by someone willing to be temporarily inconvenient. That work is not analysis. It is the precondition for analysis. And it is the beginning of actual strategic thinking rather than the rationalization of a decision already made.

examples.title: Anna Finds Twelve Studies and One Route Before the Council Vote
examples.scenario: Twelve transit study reports occupied the left side of Anna's conference table. Each one was thorough, and each one examined the same corridor from a different technical angle: soil conditions, ridership projections, cost estimates, environmental impact. The corridor had been informally designated as the preferred route before the first study was assigned. By the fifth report, Anna understood the problem: the studies were answers to questions about the preferred route, not information about whether alternative routes might be strategically superior. The analysis was comprehensive. The possibility set was one item deep. She spent the morning generating two genuine alternative routes before asking the analysis to evaluate any of them. The first concentrated service on a denser employment corridor the preferred route bypassed. The second prioritized the transit node with the weakest ridership in the existing network. Both had a real argument. Neither had been studied.
examples.whatToDo: Before using existing analysis to prepare a recommendation, generate at least two genuine alternative options with different strategic logic. Write a paragraph for each alternative describing the winning aspiration, the where-to-play choice, and the how-to-win rationale. The analysis can then compare options that exist.
examples.whyItMatters: Analysis commissioned before alternatives are generated answers questions about the preferred option, not questions about which option to prefer. A committee with one option cannot make a strategic choice; it can only approve or cancel.

examples.title: Sam Reviews the Brand Study and Realizes He Has Analysis on One Option
examples.scenario: Sam had commissioned the brand equity study six months before the digital transition deadline, reasoning that the data would drive the decision. The results were clear: high recognition among readers over fifty, flat scores among non-readers under forty, and no evidence the current brand had pull with the audience the digital strategy needed. The study was well-designed. It told Sam what the current brand was worth to people who already had it. It told him nothing about what a different positioning might be worth to people who did not. He had analysis on one option: keep the brand. He did not have a second or third option with its own logic. He could not evaluate whether to keep the brand until he had articulated what rebuilding the brand or launching a new digital identity would look like as a strategic path: which audience it targeted, what the distribution advantage would be, and how the how-to-win logic would differ.
examples.whatToDo: Before using the brand equity data to make a decision, articulate at least two alternative strategic paths as genuine options: which audience each targets, what the distribution approach would be, and what winning looks like for that audience. The study can then inform a choice between real alternatives.
examples.whyItMatters: A study that answers questions about the current option is not a substitute for generating real alternative options. Analysis can only evaluate possibilities that already exist.

examples.title: Lars Generates Two Alternatives Before the Board Gives Him an Approval Vote
examples.scenario: Lars had one option on the table six weeks before the board meeting: a full-service primary care clinic. The feasibility analysis was borderline, the recommendation inconclusive. If the board approved, the project proceeded. If they declined, the district went unserved and there was no alternative to consider. His director asked one question before he drafted the memo: what are the other options? Lars named two he had not yet analyzed. A mobile clinic rotating between three locations would cost forty percent less and reach two adjacent neighborhoods the fixed clinic could not serve. A partnership with an independent practice already operating in the district would require no capital investment and could launch in four months. Neither alternative had been studied. Both had a real argument. The difference between a strategic choice and an approval-or-cancel binary was the existence of those two alternatives.
examples.whatToDo: Before presenting a single-option analysis to a board or decision-maker, generate at least two genuine alternatives with different strategic logic. Sketch the winning aspiration, the where-to-play, and the how-to-win for each. The board can then make a strategic choice, not an approval-or-cancel decision.
examples.whyItMatters: When analysis covers only one option, decision-makers cannot choose between strategies; they can only approve or cancel. Three genuinely different options with different logic make a strategic choice possible.

examples.title: Isabel Advances to the Blank Slide and Cannot Answer the Board Member
examples.scenario: At 9:14, Isabel advanced to the slide that was supposed to show alternative curriculum models. The slide was blank. The committee had spent four months analyzing the STEM-focused curriculum: implementation costs, teacher certification requirements, projected enrollment effects, and community feedback from three town halls. The STEM decision had been made informally before the committee was formed. A board member raised her hand. 'What would the analysis look like if we had designed a different kind of school?' Isabel did not have an answer. She had an excellent analysis of one curriculum philosophy and no articulated view of what a project-based learning model or a dual-language school would look like as genuine strategic alternatives for this community. The committee had spent four months optimizing a default. The board member was asking whether anyone had done strategic thinking. The answer was visible in the blank slide.
examples.whatToDo: Before presenting a single-option curriculum analysis for board approval, generate two or three genuine alternatives and sketch the logic of each: which students it serves, what the how-to-win rationale is, and what capabilities are required. Bring those alternatives to the analysis instead of leaving the alternatives slide blank.
examples.whyItMatters: A committee asked to analyze one option produces a thorough justification, not a strategic recommendation. The board member's question exposed the gap: the analysis had begun before the possibility set was built.

examples.title: Marta Walks the Investor Through a Footnote Instead of a Strategic Path
examples.scenario: 'Walk me through what the company looks like if you take the software-only path,' the lead investor said. 'Not the risks of it. What the company actually looks like. Who the customer is, how you go to market, what winning means.' Marta had forty slides on the hardware path. She had a one-sentence footnote that said the software-only model had not been pursued due to scale limitations. She had spent six months analyzing manufacturing costs, supply chain options, distribution partnerships, and customer acquisition for the hardware path. She had not spent six hours generating what the software-only path would look like as a coherent strategy: which customers it served, why they would choose it, what the how-to-win logic was, and how the capabilities required differed from the hardware path. The investor was not asking whether the hardware path was well-analyzed. She was asking whether Marta had done the work of generating genuine options before committing to one.
examples.whatToDo: For each strategic path under consideration, build a minimum one-page sketch: the target customer, the winning aspiration, the how-to-win rationale, and the three capabilities required. A footnote that explains why a path was not pursued is not a strategic possibility.
examples.whyItMatters: A footnote explaining why an alternative was not pursued is not the same as having generated it as a genuine strategic possibility. Deep analysis of one path is not evidence of strategic thinking if the alternatives were never built out as real options.

examples.title: Jack Searches Twelve Quarters of Roadmap for a Different Strategic Path
examples.scenario: Jack went back through twelve quarters of product roadmap looking for the quarter where the team had considered a genuinely different strategic path. He found twelve quarters of feature delivery. Every sprint had addressed the most-requested items from the feedback queue. The customer data was real and the analysis was rigorous, and the product had grown slowly while two competitors launched adjacent products the team had discussed once in a whiteboard session and shelved. The team had not failed at analysis. They had failed to generate strategic options. Building the most-requested features was one path: deepen the current use case. Adding an integration marketplace was another: expand the ecosystem. Launching a lighter adjacent product was a third: extend the buyer. Each path had a different how-to-win logic, different capability requirements, and a different winning aspiration. The feature analysis had answered a question about one path without naming the other two.
examples.whatToDo: In roadmap planning, name the three genuinely different strategic paths the product could take and write a one-paragraph logic for each: which buyer it serves, what winning looks like, and what the product would need to be able to do. Then use the customer data to compare the paths, not optimize the default.
examples.whyItMatters: Feature analysis answers the question of what to build on the current path; it does not generate the question of whether a different path would win. The competitor launch that was discussed once and shelved was a strategic option that was never built as a genuine alternative.

questions.prompt: How does strategic thinking differ from analysis in the strategy development process?
choices: Strategic thinking uses qualitative methods while analysis uses quantitative data
Analysis evaluates possibilities; strategic thinking first generates them
Analysis happens before a decision is made; strategic thinking happens after
questions.explanation: Analysis can only evaluate what already exists as a possibility. The strategic thinking step, which must come first, is the generation of genuine alternatives before any analysis begins.

questions.prompt: A city transportation committee has commissioned twelve studies on one route before generating any alternative routes. Which action most directly addresses the strategic problem?
choices: Commission additional studies to validate the existing analysis before proceeding
Present the twelve studies to the council with a recommendation to approve the preferred route based on the available evidence
Generate two or three alternative routes with distinct strategic logic before using the existing analysis to compare options
questions.explanation: The problem is not the quality of the analysis but the absence of genuine alternatives. Generating alternative routes first gives the analysis something to compare. Commissioning more studies or presenting the existing analysis for approval leaves the committee with one option, not a strategic choice.

questions.prompt: When analysis runs before strategic possibilities are generated, what is the most likely result?
choices: Rationalization of the option that was already preferred, not a comparison between genuine alternatives
Discovery of options that the team would not have identified without the analytical process
A clear recommendation backed by data that the decision-maker can act on
questions.explanation: Analysis applied to a single existing option produces arguments for that option, not a comparison between genuine alternatives. This is rationalization rather than strategic thinking: the process looks thorough and defends a predetermined choice.

questions.prompt: What must a genuine strategic possibility include to be worth analyzing?
choices: A target customer, a how-to-win logic, and a rough sketch of the capabilities required
A feasibility analysis confirming the option is financially viable before it enters the comparison
Stakeholder endorsement from at least one senior decision-maker before the option is presented
questions.explanation: A genuine possibility requires at minimum a winning aspiration, a where-to-play logic, a how-to-win rationale, and a sense of the capabilities required. Financial analysis is what follows once the possibility exists, not a prerequisite for the possibility to be considered.

questions.prompt: Sam commissioned a brand equity study before deciding whether to rebrand for a digital audience. The study found high recognition among current readers and low appeal among non-readers under forty. What should Sam conclude from this?
choices: The brand has enough recognition to justify keeping it and adjusting the digital strategy to match the existing audience
He has accurate analysis on one option but must generate real alternative strategic paths before the study can inform a genuine choice
The study data is sufficient to determine that a rebrand is necessary because the recognition score among under-forty non-readers is too low
questions.explanation: The study is accurate about the present and tells Sam nothing about what alternative strategic paths would look like. He cannot choose between options until he has generated real alternatives with their own logic. The study alone can support neither keep nor rebrand as a strategic decision.

questions.prompt: Isabel's blank slide at the board presentation revealed that the committee had analyzed the STEM curriculum thoroughly but produced no alternative models. A board member asked what the analysis would look like for a different kind of school. What principle does this situation illustrate?
choices: Curriculum committees should invite board members to participate in the analysis phase to prevent gaps in the final presentation
A four-month analysis process is not long enough to generate genuine strategic alternatives for a new school model
Analysis that precedes possibility-generation produces a thorough justification for one option, not a strategic recommendation between genuine alternatives
questions.explanation: The committee's four months of work were thorough and the analysis was real. The problem was not the analysis; it was that no genuine alternatives were generated before the analysis began. The blank slide was where the strategic thinking should have started.

questions.prompt: The lead investor asked Marta to walk through what the company looks like on the software-only path, and Marta could not answer. What does this reveal about the strategic process?
choices: Climate technology investors require all strategic paths to be fully modeled before a Series A funding decision
Marta's hardware path analysis lacked sufficient detail to support a credible funding pitch
Deep analysis of one strategic path, without generating comparable views of the alternatives, is not evidence of strategic thinking
questions.explanation: Marta's hardware analysis was thorough. The gap the investor exposed was that the software-only path had never been generated as a real option with its own logic. A footnote is not a strategic alternative. The investor was looking for evidence of strategic thinking, which requires generating and comparing genuine options.

questions.prompt: Jack's roadmap review found twelve quarters of rigorous feature analysis and two competitor launches in adjacent markets the team had discussed once and shelved. Which action would have changed the outcome?
choices: Generating three genuinely different strategic paths (deepen, expand, extend) and using the customer data to compare them, not optimize the default path
Collecting more customer feedback before each quarterly roadmap cycle to ensure the feature priorities were accurate
Reviewing the competitor landscape more frequently to identify adjacent product threats earlier in the roadmap process
questions.explanation: The customer data was real and the analysis was rigorous. The problem was that the team never generated alternative strategic paths. Generating the three paths and comparing them with the existing data would have made the adjacent product option visible as a genuine strategic possibility, not a whiteboard idea that was shelved.

questions.prompt: The strategy logic flow runs in both directions rather than as a fixed sequence. What does this mean for the process of generating genuine strategic possibilities?
choices: Strategic planning should begin with management systems and work backward to the winning aspiration, since the management system is the most concrete element and starting there grounds the cascade in actionable accountability before higher-order choices are made.
Each genuine possibility should be sketched as a complete cascade across all five questions, because answering one question may require reopening a previous one

The five strategic questions can be answered in any order because they are independent of each other, since each question has its own logic and the cascade benefits from parallel work that lets teams sequence questions to their own readiness.
questions.explanation: The five questions inform each other iteratively. A how-to-win choice may reveal that the initial where-to-play was too narrow, which requires reopening the winning aspiration. This is why each genuine possibility should be a complete cascade, not a one-sentence alternative that names only one dimension of the strategy.

reviewCards.front: Why can't rigorous analysis alone produce better strategy?
reviewCards.back: Analysis can only evaluate possibilities that already exist. It cannot create them. A single option analyzed thoroughly produces a rationalization of that option, not a strategic recommendation between genuine alternatives.

reviewCards.front: What is the correct sequence: possibility-generation or analysis?
reviewCards.back: Generate first. When analysis runs before alternatives exist, the only option being studied is the one already in the room: every number, model, and slide is built to defend it. Naming two or three genuine alternatives before any analysis lets evidence actually decide between them.

reviewCards.front: Why is the strategy logic flow iterative, not a fixed linear sequence?
reviewCards.back: The five questions (winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, capabilities, management systems) inform each other. Answering one may require reopening a previous question. The logic runs in both directions, which is why each genuine option should be sketched as a complete cascade.

reviewCards.front: How can you tell whether two options are genuinely different strategic paths?
reviewCards.back: Each genuine option must have its own target customer, where-to-play logic, and how-to-win argument. Options that share the same customer field and same how-to-win but differ only in price or timing are one default with a footnote, not two genuine alternatives.

reviewCards.front: What must a genuine strategic possibility contain to be useful for analysis?
reviewCards.back: A target customer, a winning aspiration for that customer, a distinct where-to-play choice, a coherent how-to-win logic, and a rough sketch of the capabilities required to execute it. A footnote explaining why the path was not pursued is not a possibility.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to distinguish the work of generating genuine strategic possibilities from the work of analyzing them, and to sequence those activities correctly: possibilities first, analysis second. You practice generating at least two or three options with distinct logic before commissioning or applying any analysis.

ifThenPlans.context: when preparing an analysis or recommendation for a decision-maker
ifThenPlans.plan: Before starting the analysis, write down how many genuine options will be analyzed. If the answer is one, pause and generate at least two genuine alternatives with different where-to-play and how-to-win logic before proceeding. The analysis needs options to compare.

ifThenPlans.context: when a planning process has generated a lot of data but no clear recommendation
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask whether the data is attached to live options or floating without anything to evaluate. If the options slide is blank or has one option listed, the strategic thinking has not started. Name three possible paths and then return to the data.

ifThenPlans.context: when evaluating two options that feel similar
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask whether the options have different where-to-play choices or different how-to-win logic. If they target the same customer with the same approach and differ only in degree, they are one option with a footnote. Generate a genuinely different path before deciding between the two.

ifThenPlans.context: after any planning session that produced a recommendation without comparison
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask which genuine alternatives were considered and rejected. If no alternatives were generated before the analysis, the recommendation is rationalization of the preferred option. Name the option you almost never consider and sketch its logic before the decision is finalized.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before your next planning or decision meeting, write down how many genuine strategic options will be on the table. If the answer is one, spend thirty minutes generating two alternatives with different logic: a different customer, a different how-to-win, a different winning aspiration. Bring all three to the meeting and let the analysis compare them.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, each time you prepare analysis for a decision, write down the number of genuine options being analyzed before starting. If the number is one, generate at least one genuine alternative before proceeding. At the end of the week, count how many decisions had only one option when you started. That count is the size of the strategic thinking gap.

memorableLines.text: Vera had spent three weeks analyzing whether the brand identity path was viable. She had not yet spent three hours imagining what the packaging path would look like as a real strategy. That is not a gap in analysis. That is the absence of strategic thinking.
The five questions do not run in one direction. Answering where to play may reopen what winning looks like. That is not a flaw in the logic. That is what the logic is for.
The question is not whether your preferred option holds up under analysis. The question is whether the other options were real enough to lose to it.

chapters.title: Shorten Your Odds
chapters.hook: The strategy debate had been running for six weeks. Both sides had projections. Neither side had listed what would have to be true for their option to actually work.
chapters.counterintuition: The instinct under uncertainty is to gather more information until confidence arrives. The problem is that forward projection under genuine uncertainty produces more scenarios, not better decisions. The useful move is not to add more analysis but to reverse the direction: instead of projecting what might happen, ask what must be true for each option to succeed. That question produces a list of testable conditions, not a wider range of projections.
chapters.tryThisNow: For the strategic option you are most committed to right now, ask: what would have to be true for the one you are least convinced of to be the better choice? List three conditions. Check each one: evidence in hand, or assumption? The condition you cannot support is the first thing to investigate, not the last.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Shortening the odds under uncertainty means reverse engineering from a desired outcome to the specific conditions that must hold, then testing the most uncertain and most consequential conditions first rather than defending the most comfortable option.

breakdown.fastRead: Nils ran a restaurant and was weighing two options: a second location across town or a catering operation from his existing kitchen. The revenue projections looked good for both. When someone asked him to list what would have to be true for each option to succeed, the picture changed. For the catering path, he needed corporate clients at premium rates, a kitchen that could handle both service and catering without physical expansion, and a head chef willing to manage production scheduling. For the second location, he needed a neighborhood lunch crowd large enough to sustain a new spot, a manager who could run the existing location without him daily, and a landlord willing to negotiate the lease. Nils was not asking which option was safer. He was asking which assumptions each option was betting on that he could not yet verify. The catering path had two conditions he could test that week. The second location had three conditions he could not verify without signing a lease and committing a year of investment.
breakdown.deepRead:
The misunderstanding that blocks clear decisions under uncertainty is the belief that more analysis will eventually produce enough confidence to act. The problem is that forward projection under genuine uncertainty produces more scenarios, not better decisions. The output is a wider range of possibilities and the same unresolved disagreement about which option to choose.

The what-would-have-to-be-true approach works in the opposite direction. Instead of projecting forward from available data, it works backward from a desired outcome. For each strategic option under consideration, the question is: what must be true for this option to succeed? The answer is a list of conditions, not a single probability estimate. Some conditions can be verified now with existing data. Some require a small test before the full commitment. Some cannot be resolved without committing to the option and accepting the uncertainty. Instead of asking which option is right, ask what would have to be true for each option to work. The conditions that neither side can agree on are the ones worth testing before committing to either.

That is where to put the next week's effort.

The practical sequence is to list the conditions for each option, rank them by consequence, and identify which high-consequence conditions are currently supported only by assumption rather than evidence. A condition that is uncertain but low-consequence can wait. A condition that is certain but high-consequence is a known constraint, not a risk. The most dangerous condition is the one that is both most consequential and treated as assumed, not yet verified.
breakdown.fullRead:
Forward projection under uncertainty produces a useful feeling and a dangerous output. The feeling is rigor: multiple scenarios, probability estimates, sensitivity analyses. The output is a wider range of projections attached to the same unresolved strategic question. Adding another scenario does not resolve which option to choose; it extends the analysis phase and defers the commitment. The what-would-have-to-be-true approach changes the question being asked and, as a result, changes what the team does next.

The six examples above share a structural feature. In each case, the strategic debate was stuck because both sides were defending positions, not listing conditions. Sarah and her co-founder were arguing about which product path was safer. Matt's council was arguing about whether the repair estimate was credible. Julien's team was arguing about which market was larger. In each case, the stuck argument converted into a tractable question as soon as someone asked: what would have to be true for this option to work? The question produced a list. The list had items with different evidence quality. The items with the least support became the first tests.

A condition is useful when it is written specifically enough that a test can touch it. 'The market will respond well' is not a condition; it is a hope. 'At least twelve of thirty trial users will invite a teammate in week one' is a condition. 'The neighborhood will support a second location' is not testable. 'The block has at least eight hundred weekday lunch visitors who do not yet have a dedicated option' is a condition. The specificity requirement is not pedantic. It is what makes the condition honest, not merely reassuring.

Consider the option you are currently leaning toward on a decision you are carrying right now. What would have to be true for the option you are not leaning toward to actually be the better choice? Write the conditions for that option down. Now look at each condition and ask: do you have evidence for this, or are you assuming it? The conditions you are assuming but cannot yet verify are the ones your choice is actually resting on. If those conditions were false, would you still choose the same option? That is the question the analysis has not yet answered.

The uncertainty does not go away when you choose. But you can choose to test the most uncertain conditions before you commit, rather than discovering them after.

The order in which conditions are tested matters as much as the list itself. The temptation is to test the easiest condition first, because an easy test feels like progress and produces an early confirmation. But the easy condition is rarely the consequential one. The condition worth testing first is the one that, if false, would change the decision. A small pilot on the riskiest condition before the full commitment is more valuable than a large study on conditions that will not change the outcome.

Shortening the odds is not the same as eliminating uncertainty. A competitor can move after the commitment is made. A supplier can fail. Market behavior can shift in ways that no condition list predicted. The value of the what-would-have-to-be-true approach is not that it makes surprise impossible. It is that it converts avoidable ignorance into early tests. The surprises that remain are genuine surprises. The assumptions that were testable before the commitment are no longer acceptable as reasons for failure after it.

examples.title: Sarah Converts a Co-Founder Argument Into a List of Testable Conditions
examples.scenario: 'You keep saying B2B is safer,' Sarah's co-founder said. 'You haven't said what would have to be true for B2C to win.' Sarah paused. That was the question she had been avoiding. She wrote it at the top of the whiteboard: what must be true for B2C to work? Her co-founder started listing: high organic word-of-mouth so the acquisition cost stays low, conversion from free to paid that is faster than the category average, and a viral loop that works without influencer spending. Sarah wrote each condition down. Then she asked which of those conditions they could test in the next six weeks without committing to the full build. The argument stopped being about who was right. It became about which conditions were most uncertain and what the cheapest honest test looked like.
examples.whatToDo: When a strategic debate is stuck between two positions, stop arguing which option is correct and start listing what must be true for each option to succeed. Then identify which conditions are testable before full commitment and run those tests first.
examples.whyItMatters: Turning conditions into testable propositions changes the conversation from defending positions to investigating evidence. The co-founders were not disagreeing about facts; they were assuming different conditions. Making the assumptions explicit is the first step to resolving them.

examples.title: Matt Lists What Would Have to Be True Before the City Council Votes on the Bridge
examples.scenario: At 2:15, Matt advanced to the slide comparing repair at four million and new build at twenty-two million. A council member in the third row raised her hand before he finished. 'Walk me through what would have to be true for the repair to be the right choice,' she said. Matt listed the conditions: the structural assessment must confirm twenty-year life, the foundation must be sound enough to hold the repaired load, and the contractor must be able to hold the budget through winter construction. The council member asked which of those three conditions they actually knew versus assumed. One was known. Two were assumed. The committee had a vote scheduled for Thursday and two conditions that had not yet been tested.
examples.whatToDo: Before bringing a cost comparison to a decision-maker, list the specific conditions each option requires and mark which are supported by evidence versus which are currently assumed. The assumed conditions on the lower-cost option are often the ones that determine whether the savings are real.
examples.whyItMatters: The council member's question converted a cost debate into a condition inventory. The two assumed conditions were the actual risk in the repair option, not the cost difference. Testing them before the vote was cheaper than discovering them during construction.

examples.title: Julien Discovers That Three Conditions Drive the Urban Launch Differently Than Assumed
examples.scenario: Which launch market was the right choice when the company could only afford one? Julien had predicted the urban market would win the argument on size alone. He asked his team to list what would have to be true for each path to succeed before the budget was allocated. The urban launch required a performance marketing budget the company did not have, a retail placement that would take six months to negotiate, and a customer acquisition cost below a threshold the company had never achieved in any market. The regional launch required word-of-mouth velocity that a similar product had demonstrated the previous year and a distribution partnership the company already had in that geography. The size argument had been true. The condition argument changed the decision.
examples.whatToDo: Before choosing between two launch paths based on market size, list the specific conditions each path requires and check which conditions have supporting evidence from prior experience. The path with better evidence quality on its load-bearing conditions is often the one worth trying first.
examples.whyItMatters: Market size is an outcome, not a condition. Julien's team had been debating which market was bigger when the real question was which conditions they already had evidence for. The condition list converted a size debate into an evidence inventory.

examples.title: Diego Finds the Single Most Uncertain Condition and Designs a Pilot Around It
examples.scenario: Two study design proposals sat on the research committee table: the large randomized controlled trial on the left, labeled three years and full budget; the adaptive trial on the right, labeled eighteen months and sixty percent of the cost. Before: Diego framed the choice as a budget decision and the committee debated timelines. After: he asked what would have to be true for the adaptive trial to succeed and the conditions changed the conversation. The adaptive design required the early signal to be clean enough to adjust the protocol without introducing bias. That single condition was the most uncertain and the most consequential. It was also testable with a small preliminary study before either full design was committed. The committee stopped debating the budget and started planning the pilot.
examples.whatToDo: Before choosing between a faster, cheaper option and a slower, more expensive one, list the conditions for each and identify the single most uncertain condition on the faster option. If that condition is testable with a small pilot, run the pilot before committing to either full design.
examples.whyItMatters: The cost advantage of the adaptive trial was real only if the early signal condition held. That condition was testable before the commitment. Running a budget debate without first identifying the most uncertain condition meant the committee was evaluating the wrong question.

examples.title: Petra Shifts the Acquisitions Committee From Manuscript Evaluation to Condition Testing
examples.scenario: Petra had reviewed the comparison document three times: prose quality, marketability, category fit, all rated for both manuscripts. The established author scored reliably. The debut scored exceptionally on prose and unevenly on everything else. She put the comparison document aside and asked a different question: what would have to be true for the debut to reach its target? The conditions were specific. The exceptional reader response must hold across a broader test group, not just the original early readers. The social media following must represent genuine engagement, not inflated counts. The category must have room for a new voice in the current season. Petra could verify two of the three before the committee meeting. She brought the condition list instead of the comparison document.
examples.whatToDo: Before making an acquisition decision based on evaluation criteria, ask what conditions must hold for the riskier option to succeed. Identify which conditions are verifiable before the commitment and gather that evidence before the decision meeting.
examples.whyItMatters: The comparison document ranked both manuscripts on the same criteria and could not resolve the debate. The condition list gave the committee something actionable: two conditions worth verifying before committing the budget to either manuscript.

examples.title: Frida Prepares for the Investment Committee's Question About Site B's Conditions
examples.scenario: You are preparing both site presentations for the investment committee and you already know the question that will come. Site B's pro forma is strong, but the committee will ask: what would have to be true for this site to be the right choice? Frida ran through the conditions before the meeting. Neighborhood demand growth must continue at its current pace through the three-year construction period. The zoning approval must proceed on the projected timeline without the variance that would add a year. The anchor tenant must commit before construction begins, not after. The pro forma assumed all three. The first condition was supported by two years of demand data. The second was assumed. The third was the condition that had sunk three previous transitional-neighborhood projects in the region. She knew which condition to test before the committee meeting and what the test would cost.
examples.whatToDo: Before presenting a business case to an investment committee, anticipate the 'what would have to be true' question for the riskier option and prepare condition-specific answers. Identify which conditions are assumed versus supported and have a plan for the most uncertain one.
examples.whyItMatters: The pro forma comparison made both sites look attractive. The condition inventory showed that Site B's advantage rested on three assumptions, one of which had a documented history of causing project failures. That condition, not the pro forma, was the real decision variable.

questions.prompt: Why does the 'what would have to be true' question help teams make better decisions under uncertainty?
choices: To identify which strategic option has the most supporting data before the decision is made
To determine which team members have the most confidence in each strategic option
To convert forward projections into a list of specific conditions that each option requires in order to succeed
questions.explanation: The question reverses the direction of analysis: instead of projecting forward from available data, it works backward from a desired outcome to the conditions that must hold. The output is a list of conditions, not a confidence ranking.

questions.prompt: Two co-founders are arguing about whether to build a B2B or B2C product. Sarah asks: 'What would have to be true for the B2C path to win?' Her co-founder lists three conditions. What should the team do next?
choices: Analyze the market size for each option to determine which has more revenue potential
Identify which conditions are testable in the next six weeks without committing to the full build, and run those tests first
Survey potential customers to determine which product type they would prefer before making the decision
questions.explanation: Once conditions are listed, the next step is to sort them by testability before full commitment. The conditions that can be tested cheaply before the major investment are the ones that should be tested first. Market size analysis and customer surveys are useful but do not test the specific conditions that could change the decision.

questions.prompt: Matt presented a bridge repair option at four million dollars versus a new build at twenty-two million. A council member asked what would have to be true for the repair to be the right choice. Matt identified three conditions: one supported by evidence and two assumed. What does this reveal?
choices: The cost comparison was the wrong frame; the two assumed conditions are the actual risk in the repair option and should be tested before the vote
The repair option is likely to cost more than projected because assumed conditions often lead to budget overruns
The council should delay the vote until the contractor can provide a binding cost guarantee for all three conditions
questions.explanation: The assumed conditions are where the cost advantage of the repair option can fail. Testing them before the vote is cheaper than discovering them during construction. The cost comparison gave the council a false sense of which decision was lower risk.

questions.prompt: Julien's team found that the urban launch required three conditions his company had never met, while the regional launch required two conditions supported by existing evidence. Which action follows from this finding?
choices: Commission a new study on whether the urban market conditions could be met before making a final decision
Split the launch budget between both markets to test the conditions for both simultaneously
Choose the regional launch path because it has better evidence quality on its load-bearing conditions
questions.explanation: The condition inventory showed that the regional launch had supporting evidence for its key conditions while the urban launch required capabilities the company had never demonstrated. That evidence quality difference, not market size, is the strategically relevant finding. The regional path has better-supported conditions.

questions.prompt: Diego's research committee was debating between an eighteen-month adaptive trial and a three-year randomized controlled trial. After listing the conditions each design required, the committee found the single most uncertain condition for the adaptive trial was testable with a small preliminary study. What is the correct next step?
choices: Run the preliminary study to test the most uncertain condition before committing to either full design
Proceed with the randomized controlled trial because it has fewer uncertain conditions
Request additional budget to fund both designs simultaneously so the committee can evaluate the results in parallel
questions.explanation: When the most uncertain condition for the riskier option is testable before full commitment, the correct step is to run that test. The preliminary study provides evidence on the condition that determines whether the faster path is viable, at a fraction of the cost of committing to either full design.

questions.prompt: Petra reframed the manuscript acquisition debate from 'which manuscript is better' to 'what would have to be true for the debut to hit its target.' She found two of the three required conditions were verifiable before the committee meeting. What principle does this illustrate?
choices: Evaluation criteria are not useful for acquisition decisions because they cannot capture the conditions that drive commercial outcomes after publication, since manuscript quality is a separate dimension from market success and rubrics conflate the two.
Reframing a comparative evaluation as a condition inventory reveals which conditions are testable before the commitment and gives the decision a concrete next step

Condition inventory is most useful for decisions with objective measurable outcomes, while manuscript acquisition requires the comparative aesthetic and market judgment that conditions cannot fully capture without flattening editorial expertise.
questions.explanation: The comparison document could not resolve the debate because it ranked both manuscripts on criteria that did not reveal the specific conditions driving the risk. The condition list gave the committee something actionable: evidence to gather before the meeting, not subjective ratings to debate.

questions.prompt: Frida identified that Site B's pro forma rested on three conditions: two supported by data and one with a documented history of causing project failures in similar neighborhoods. What is the most strategically sound way to present this to the investment committee?
choices: Recommend Site A because the presence of any high-risk assumed condition makes Site B's pro forma unreliable regardless of the other conditions
Present the condition inventory with the evidence quality for each condition and a specific plan for testing the most uncertain one before committing to Site B
Present both pro formas with sensitivity analysis showing the committee what happens if each condition fails
questions.explanation: The condition inventory gives the committee the actual information driving the decision: which conditions are supported and which are assumed. The plan to test the most uncertain condition before committing shows the committee a path to reduce the risk before committing, not simply accept or reject the site. Recommending Site A on the basis of one uncertain condition ignores the possibility that the condition is testable. Sensitivity analysis shows what happens if conditions fail but does not reduce the uncertainty.

questions.prompt: The planning team has been asked to choose between two options. The team has rotated through the same debate for three months without converging. What is the right strategic move?
choices: Commission additional market research to resolve the disagreement with more data
Escalate the decision to senior leadership who can resolve the impasse with a final call
Ask each side to list the conditions their option requires, then identify which are assumed rather than supported by evidence
questions.explanation: When analysis has not resolved a strategic disagreement, the problem is usually that both sides are defending positions, not examining conditions. Asking each side to list specific conditions converts the debate into an evidence inventory and identifies the assumptions that are actually driving the disagreement.

questions.prompt: Why is the order in which conditions are tested strategically important?
choices: The condition that is both most consequential and most uncertain should be tested first, because a failed test on that condition is the one that should change the decision

Testing easier conditions first builds team confidence and momentum before addressing the harder ones, since early wins create the organizational commitment to keep going when later tests reveal more difficult conditions.

Conditions should be tested in the order they were identified to maintain a consistent process, since following the original identification order preserves the team's record of how the analysis evolved and supports later auditability.
questions.explanation: Testing easy conditions first produces early confirmation but avoids the assumption that most threatens the decision. The condition worth testing first is the one that, if false, would change the choice. Easy tests on low-consequence conditions do not improve the odds; they generate activity that avoids the real question.

reviewCards.front: What does the 'what would have to be true' question produce that forward projection does not?
reviewCards.back: A list of specific conditions that each option requires in order to succeed, rather than a wider range of projections. The conditions can be ranked by consequence and evidence quality, which the projections cannot.

reviewCards.front: How do you sort a condition list once you have written it?
reviewCards.back: Rank by consequence (if this condition is false, how much does it matter?) and by current evidence quality (supported by data, or assumed?). The conditions that are most consequential and least supported by evidence are the ones to test first.

reviewCards.front: What makes a condition testable rather than vague?
reviewCards.back: A testable condition is written specifically enough that a test can touch it. 'The market will respond well' is not testable. 'At least twelve of thirty trial users will invite a teammate in week one' is testable. The specificity is what makes the test honest.

reviewCards.front: When a strategic debate is stuck between two positions, what does the 'what would have to be true' question change?
reviewCards.back: It converts the debate from defending positions to listing conditions. The conditions that both sides disagree about are the assumptions driving the disagreement, not the facts. Making the assumptions explicit is the first step to resolving them through evidence.

reviewCards.front: Does the 'what would have to be true' approach eliminate uncertainty?
reviewCards.back: No. Competitors can move, suppliers can fail, and behavior can shift after the commitment. The value is that it converts avoidable ignorance into early tests. The surprises that remain after testing the most uncertain conditions are genuine surprises, not assumptions that could have been checked.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to reverse engineer from a desired strategic outcome to the specific conditions that must hold, then rank those conditions by consequence and evidence quality so the most uncertain and most consequential ones get tested before the full commitment is made.

ifThenPlans.context: when a strategic debate is stuck between two options and more analysis is not resolving it
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask each side to list what must be true for their preferred option to succeed. The conditions that both sides disagree about are the assumptions driving the disagreement. Run a test on the most uncertain one before continuing the debate.

ifThenPlans.context: when preparing a recommendation for a decision-maker
ifThenPlans.plan: Before finalizing the recommendation, list the conditions the preferred option requires and mark which are supported by evidence versus assumed. Present both the recommendation and the condition inventory so the decision-maker can see what has and has not been verified.

ifThenPlans.context: when a team is about to commit budget to a strategic option
ifThenPlans.plan: Ask what would have to be true for the option that is not being chosen to be the better decision. List the conditions for that option and check the evidence quality. The conditions you cannot support are the ones to investigate before the budget is committed.

ifThenPlans.context: when facing a decision with significant uncertainty
ifThenPlans.plan: Write the conditions for each option. Identify the single most uncertain condition for the option that appears most attractive. Ask what it would cost to test that condition before the full commitment. If the test is cheaper than the cost of being wrong, run it first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take a decision you are currently carrying and write the conditions for each option: what must be true for each one to succeed. Mark each condition as either supported by evidence or currently assumed. Name the one assumed condition that would most change your thinking if it turned out to be false. That is the first thing to investigate.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, each time you hear a strategic debate stuck on positions, ask what would have to be true for each side to be correct. Write the conditions for both positions. At the end of the week, review which conditions were testable and which were not. The testable conditions that nobody tested are the places where the team could have shortened its odds.
